1. From AI-Assisted Coding to Spec-Driven Development

1.1 Starting with a prompt

More software work now begins with a description than with a blank file. You describe the behaviour you want, and a model returns code, a test, a documentation draft, or a refactoring suggestion. The request can be a sentence or a page. You can paste the response into the project and try it. That is the new starting point, and it changes how quickly a first result appears.

The effect is largest when the task is bounded. A prototype, an isolated utility, a converter, or a small feature with a clear input and output gives the model enough context to produce something useful. Trying an approach costs less, so you try more approaches. That is a real gain, and it is not limited to trivial work. It is only strongest where the boundaries are visible.

Speed is not the same as quality. Code that arrives quickly can still ignore the project's conventions. It can duplicate an abstraction that already exists. It can solve the immediate request in a way that fits badly with the surrounding design. It may run and still be hard to maintain. Running is a low standard. Whether the result is right is a separate question.

The first way of working is simple. You explain the feature, ask for an implementation, paste the result into the project, and try it. If it fails, you describe the failure and ask for another attempt. If it passes, you may keep it and continue with the next task. The loop is prompt, generate, paste, test, and repeat. It is often enough to produce a first version that you can look at.

That loop is really useful. It gives fast feedback and makes starting cheaper. It also makes it easy to explore a library or an API before you commit to a design. It is a good way to build a throwaway prototype, a small script, or a rough feature that you intend to rewrite. The speed is not a trick. It changes what you are willing to try.

The limitation is in the input. The result is only as good as the request and the assumptions that the model brings to it. The model infers a missing behaviour instead of asking about it. It chooses an unsuitable architecture because it has no knowledge of the project's architecture, so it guesses from what it does know. It ignores project conventions because they were never in the prompt. Nothing in the result shows which part is a guess and which part is a decision. Every piece of information that the request does not contain lets the model guess, and those guesses end up in the code. None of this requires the model to be careless. It follows from working with an incomplete description. Not all of the missing information is context that someone forgot to provide. A requirement can correctly say nothing about things that are not requirements — the order of operations, the wording of a message, the internal structure of a component. Each of those gaps is a decision that someone still has to make. When a model fills one, the result is a guess inside the code. When a developer resolves one in conversation, the answer is lost when the session ends.

1.2 Discussing the change before writing code

Direct generation is still a legitimate way of working, but it leaves no lasting statement of intent. When the first result survives, the next improvement is a conversation about the implementation before any code is requested. You and the model discuss what the change should do, what it must fit into, and which trade-offs are acceptable. No code is written yet. The request becomes a shared proposal instead of a single instruction.

The conversation covers the decisions that code would otherwise make without anyone noticing:

  • what problem the change solves and what behaviour it should produce;
  • what existing code, interfaces and constraints it has to fit;
  • which design options exist and what each one gives up;
  • which edge cases, failure modes and security concerns matter;
  • what tests or acceptance criteria will show that it works;
  • how the work should be ordered into steps.

When you discuss those decisions first, a vague request becomes shared understanding. The purpose is to close the information gaps before the model fills them with guesses. Ambiguity becomes visible while it is still cheap to resolve. You can question assumptions before they are built into the source. Rework falls because the shape of the change is agreed before it is built. The gain depends on the quality of the conversation. A discussion that never reaches a decision is only a longer prompt.

Consider a request as ordinary as "add CSV export". Which records should be exported? Which columns? Does the current filter apply, or does export ignore it? How should dates, numbers and text be formatted? Who is allowed to export what? What happens when the result is too large to build in memory? What should the file be called, and should the same request produce the same file twice? The request is one sentence, but the implementation is a set of decisions. People often describe a requirement as clear, testable or well-specified. These labels are adjectives, and they do not find a problem. A requirement passes the test when a concrete question about it can be answered, and not only discussed.

1.3 What the conversation loses

The conversation is better than the prompt, but it is still a conversation. Its value is in the chat, and it is usually lost when the chat ends. You may have produced an excellent plan, but the plan is hard to find again later, and the conversation is not a project artifact. The next person sees the code, not the reasoning that produced it.

A later reader needs information that only the conversation held:

  • why the change was made;
  • which alternatives were rejected, and why;
  • what was in scope and what was left out on purpose;
  • which constraints and project rules applied;
  • what must not break;
  • how the result was validated.

The same developer a week later is also a later reader. Memory is not a reliable interface.

Without a stable description, the system drifts. Drift is the slow growth of a difference between what the system is supposed to do and what its code, tests and documents now say. Each change is made from a local understanding of the system, and these local understandings add up. A specification can serve as the reference that shows drift so that it can be corrected. This works only if the specification itself is reviewed and maintained. An outdated reference makes drift harder to see, not easier.

Review becomes weaker under the same pressure. A reviewer sees a diff: lines added, lines removed, tests changed. The reviewer does not see the intent behind the change. Without a lasting statement of purpose, the reviewer reconstructs it from the code, the commit message or memory. Exclusions made on purpose are especially hard to see: the reviewer cannot tell whether something was left out on purpose or forgotten. The review then checks the implementation instead of the change. Only a record of the exclusion makes the difference visible. A scope boundary stated in a conversation is lost when the conversation ends. A scope boundary written into an artifact can be seen, questioned, and maintained.

Direct generation answers a narrow question: can we do this? It does not answer what should work or why it should work that way. It does not answer how the work should be approached or which constraints apply. It does not answer what behaviour is acceptable and how that behaviour will be verified. Those answers are not a better prompt. They are a lasting record of intent that can be reviewed. Different technologies and practices can supply that record. The next paragraphs examine attempts to improve generation, and then ask what such a record must do.

1.4 Why better context is not enough

Several techniques can improve the context available to direct generation:

  • retrieval over design decisions, specifications, code and past changes;
  • tool servers or protocols, such as MCP, that expose repositories, issue trackers, CI and monitoring;
  • persistent project instruction files, such as AGENTS.md, that are read at the start of a session;
  • repository search and dependency context;
  • automated tests, linters and type checks whose results are fed back into the loop.

Each technique gives the model more to work with. None of them, alone, decides what the work should be.

These techniques are worth using, but alone they do not solve the main problem. People most often assume that the instruction file is valuable. It tells an agent what the project expects. But where such files have been compared with having none, the work has not become better: what changed was how the agent worked, not what it produced. A context file passes on what a team already knows. It does not raise quality. Retrieval sees only what someone stored, and only in the form in which they stored it. Tool access gives the current state, not lasting intent. Session context is a selection, not the whole history. The conversation, the assumptions and the rejected alternatives are still lost when the session closes, unless someone writes them down. Files can keep what the session loses, and written records are the basis of the way of working that follows. But a collection of files built by hand will not match a framework that defines the artifacts, their relationships and their checks.

A specification can serve as that written reference. Tools, agents and people can work from it, and it can be reviewed and corrected. It is not an authority that is always right. A wrong specification is a defect to fix, not a truth to obey. So the question is not whether a document exists. The question is whether it keeps the intent that the work needs, and whether the team keeps it correct.

1.5 What the work needs

These failures suggest a set of needs, not a feature list. The first group is about keeping intent and context. A lasting record should keep the intent of a change: why it is needed, what it should achieve, and what is excluded. It should make key information available later without the old transcript. It should capture the general rules that apply to change, such as architecture, standards, testing, security, accessibility and error handling. It should describe the complete application, not only the part being changed. And it should keep current behaviour separate from the proposed change.

The second group is about how the work is reviewed, traced, delivered and validated. The record should be reviewable as an artifact, not only as a conversation. It should support traceability from a requirement to design decisions, tasks, tests and implementation. It should allow incremental delivery, so that work can be split into changes that can be reviewed. It should support validation, not only generation: acceptance criteria and tests need a basis for checking the result. The tests alone are not that basis. A test can pass and still measure nothing that was asked for, because no test states which claim it is meant to decide. Only a requirement written down beforehand gives a test something to be measured against. Only such a requirement says what passing is supposed to mean. And the record should stay lightweight and in proportion to the change, because people abandon a record that costs more than the change it describes.

1.6 From needs to spec-driven development

One family of practices responds to those needs. It makes intent explicit and treats the specification as an active artifact. In spec-driven development (SDD), requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria and validation are made explicit before and during implementation. The specification guides planning, implementation, testing and validation. It is a living reference, not a project history, and it is expected to change when the work teaches something new.

OpenSpec is one concrete implementation. It organizes work as a change proposal, capability specifications, a design and a task list. Its specs/ directory holds the current behaviour of the system. Its changes/ directory holds proposed modifications and the artifacts that describe them. Those are conventions, not requirements of spec-driven development. Another implementation could use different names and a different file layout and still do the same work.

The needs are the test, not the tool. Another spec-driven tool or a team's own practice may use different names, different artifacts and a different way of working. The question to ask is whether it does these things: keeps intent, makes information available, captures general rules, describes the system, and keeps current behaviour separate from proposed change. It must also support review, traceability, incremental delivery and validation, and stay in proportion to the change. In this argument, OpenSpec can be replaced. If a practice meets the needs, the names matter less than the record.

1.7 What SDD costs

The cost of a record cannot be calculated exactly, but its form is clear, and the cost comes before anything is paid back. Planning takes time and tokens. The attention it needs competes with the attention that the rest of the work needs. The record is work of its own: it has to be read, reviewed and kept current. Every hour spent on it is an hour not spent on something else.

Most of the cost is not the writing. It is the deciding. The questions that a record has to answer are the questions that the work would otherwise have left to whoever implemented it, and answering them takes judgment. A page of prose is cheap. The expensive part is the hour spent deciding what the page should say, and that hour is spent whether or not anyone ever writes the page.

What a record saves is rework that did not happen, so the saving is hard to see. A change that goes well leaves no trace of the version that would have gone wrong. So the benefit never appears as a line that anyone can point at. The cost does appear: it is in the session, in the review and in the record.

The cost is not small. In comparisons where the two approaches were run side by side on the same tasks, one approach wrote a specification, a plan and a task list before implementing. It spent many times the tokens and the elapsed time of a single free-form request. Its gain in passing tests was real, and far smaller than that multiple. A benchmark is not a team, so the comparison does not set the exact price. It sets the order of magnitude. This is a purchase with a visible cost, not a small extra step.

A record comes in sizes, and the size sets the price. It can be a paragraph in a change description, a specification kept beside the code, or the artifact from which the code is generated. Each size needs more discipline than the one before, and has to stay correct for longer. So choosing a size means choosing what the work costs.

The person who pays for a record is usually not the person who gains from it. The effort falls on whoever writes it. The saving falls on whoever reads it later, and that reader never sees the hour it cost. For this reason, a practice can be worth keeping for one person and still meet resistance from the team around that person. A team that wants the saving has to say what deserves a record. If each person decides alone, the answers differ, and the record becomes a different thing in every change.

1.8 What SDD gives back

In return, three things are no longer lost. Rework is avoided: the decisions that implementation would have forced were made before it. Review gets something to review: the reviewer sees the intent and the exclusions, not only the diff. And the next change gets a starting point, because it begins from a written reference instead of from someone's memory of the last conversation.

The size of that return cannot be measured from the outside, and it should be read as an estimate. Part of it comes from the record. Part comes from the models being better at the same task than they were before. Part comes from stating the goal before delegating the work, which a careful conversation would also produce. What remains is a judgement: the record is worth its cost to the people who keep it, and the size of the return is not established.

That judgement is not a measurement, and the measurements that exist are discouraging. Specifications have been compared with no specifications across tens of thousands of changes. There, the difference in defects and in rework has been hard to find at all. The association that does appear is explained by the difficulty of the work that gets specified. Such a comparison sees specification documents as they are stored in repositories — a ticket reference, a page beside the code. It does not see the practice of writing one, and that practice is what this chapter argues for. So the comparison does not show that a record fails to help. It shows that the help has not been visible where people expected it to be easiest to see. That is an argument for choosing where to write a record, not for abandoning the practice.

1.9 When SDD is worth its cost

SDD is strong where intent, constraints and verification matter. Feature development, behavioural changes, integrations, refactors with risk, and security-sensitive work all benefit from a record. The record says what should happen and how it will be checked. Collaboration among humans and agents also benefits, because the record is the shared reference that both can work from. These are defaults, not a universal rule.

SDD is less useful when the specification costs more than the change is worth. A quick experiment, a one-off script, an exploratory spike, a trivial fix, or an early prototype may need only a conversation. The purpose of such a prototype is to learn what to build. Writing a full record for such work can slow the learning that the work exists to produce. The list is not complete, and simple work is not a defect.

None of this removes engineering judgment. A specification can be wrong, incomplete, too rigid or too abstract. The team still has to review the requirements, question the design, write meaningful tests, inspect the code and maintain the specification. SDD reduces guessing, but it does not move responsibility to a document or a tool. The human is still responsible for the artifacts being right.

SDD does not replace direct AI coding or conversational exploration. The chapter has described three ways of working: direct generation, explain mode — the conversation before code — and spec-driven development. Each has legitimate uses, and the situation should decide the choice, not an ideology. The table below gives a better default for several situations. Three questions produce it. How long does the result have to live? How many people or agents will work on it? What would a wrong guess cost? The three ways of working differ in whether a record is used. These questions decide how large that record should be. "Better default" does not mean the only option.

Situation Better default
Explore an idea or learn an API Direct generation or explain mode
Build a disposable prototype Direct generation; keep light notes if it survives
Fix a small isolated bug Explain mode; add a lightweight change record if the fix grows
Change user-facing behaviour SDD
Work on a critical workflow or integration SDD
Make an architectural decision SDD, especially with recorded rationale
Work across multiple sessions, people or agents SDD
Need reviewable intent and traceability SDD

These three ways of working are not levels that you leave behind as you advance. They suit work that must last for different lengths of time. Direct generation is fastest when the result can be tried at once. Explain mode is better when the request has to be understood before code exists. Spec-driven development is worth its cost when intent has to survive the session, be reviewed by someone else, or be traced from a requirement to a test.

The three ways differ in how they treat the information that the model does not have. Direct generation leaves the model to guess. Explain mode resolves some of the gaps before code exists, but its answers stay in the conversation. A lasting record keeps those answers where a later session, reviewer or agent can find them, so the next change does not start from a partial memory. Understanding starts in the conversation, but it does not stay there. A specification, a change record and the tests that decide them are one way to keep that reference correct. So the rule is not "always specify" but "preserve enough context for the work". Use the lightest process that keeps the model from guessing about what matters, and that keeps the context needed to build, review and maintain the result.

2. The Cornerstones of Spec-Driven Development

The conversation in chapter 1 settled the intent. When it ended, nothing had been written down. A good discussion is not a durable record. The next step is to name the principles that make a record durable enough to guide work, and this chapter does that. Spec-driven development (SDD) is a disciplined way to build software. In SDD, an explicit, versioned specification steers planning, implementation, testing and maintenance. It is not a programming language, and it does not replace engineering judgment. It is a way to make intent available to the people and tools that have to act on it.

2.1 What software development already solved

The gap between an idea and a working system is old. Software development has built practices to close it:

  • requirements engineering describes what a system should do, for whom, and under which constraints. It separates functional behaviour from quality attributes such as performance, security and usability;
  • architecture and design describe the system's structure, its components and their responsibilities, its interfaces and its important trade-offs;
  • version control records how the code changed. It allows parallel work and makes a change reviewable;
  • issue trackers explain why work is needed, who owns it and which need it serves;
  • automated tests encode expected behaviour and protect against regressions;
  • code review adds a second reader, who checks correctness, security and maintainability;
  • documentation keeps knowledge after the conversation that produced it has ended. It often becomes outdated when it is written after implementation.

These practices remain valuable. SDD does not discard them, and it does not pretend to have invented them. It changes what organizes them. The specification is not written once and then left unused. It stays active while the work is planned, implemented, tested and maintained. The change is in the organizing principle, not in the list of practices.

2.2 What AI changed

Chapter 1 described what happens when a model can turn a sentence into a plausible implementation. This chapter draws a narrower consequence from it. A human who writes code carries a lot of context without stating it: experience, project conventions, architectural constraints and a sense of the users. When a model generates code, that context has to be made explicit. Otherwise the model fills the gap with a guess. The faster the code arrives, the more a wrong assumption costs.

The model does not guess without context. A harness is everything around a language model that turns it into an agent. It includes the loop that feeds results back to the model, the tools the model can call, the context and instructions it receives, and the permissions that limit what it may do. In a coding agent, the model proposes an edit. The harness applies the edit, runs the tests and returns the output for the next step. Some people use the word more narrowly, for a product. Others use it more broadly, for everything a team assembles around one. This chapter uses it for the whole runtime that connects the model to the work. What the harness supplies decides how much of the gap remains.

A single plausible answer is not the same as the right answer. A model can generate several plausible answers. It cannot know which one matches the team's intent unless that intent is available. Two sessions can follow different conventions. One may use the pattern that the project already has, and the next may invent a new one. The response is not a better prompt. The response is a shared, explicit reference: requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria and project context are treated as artifacts of their own. The specification is that reference for intent. It stays that reference only as long as it is reviewed and corrected.

2.3 Why the order of work changes

Traditional documentation often describes a system after it has been built. Or it describes a plan that nobody updates once implementation begins. In an AI-assisted way of working, this weakness is more visible. An agent may use outdated or incomplete context, and produce code that fits the document rather than the system. The problem is not new, but finding it late costs more.

SDD changes the order of work:

  1. Describe the problem and the desired outcome.
  2. Specify behaviour, constraints and acceptance criteria.
  3. Plan the technical approach.
  4. Break the work into reviewable tasks.
  5. Implement with AI and human collaboration.
  6. Validate the implementation against the specification.
  7. Update the specification so it continues to describe the system accurately.

The order is a discipline. It does not claim that the intent is complete before the first line of code exists. What a specification is missing often becomes clear only while the work is in progress. That is why the last step is part of the method, and not an extra added at the end.

The order creates a feedback loop between intent and implementation. Code is no longer the only reliable record of what the system does. The specification becomes a living description of expected behaviour, and code, tests and documentation stay consistent with it. The loop is not automatic. Someone has to notice that the implementation taught something new. That person then has to carry it back into the specification.

2.4 The cornerstones

SDD frameworks differ in terminology and way of working, but most share a small set of basic ideas. These ideas are the cornerstones. They are principles that hold whatever tool or names a team uses. They are not a list of product features. Chapter 1 derived ten needs from the gaps that direct generation and conversation leave. The cornerstones are those needs, restated as principles that a way of working can be checked against. Three differences are on purpose. Proportionality is not a cornerstone, because it decides how much record to write, not what the record contains. Living documentation and human control do appear as cornerstones. The reason is that chapter 1 stated them as rules of judgment rather than as needs, and a way of working has to carry them.

Cornerstone Meaning How it decays
Explicit intent The purpose, scope, users and expected outcome of a change are written down before implementation. The work done no longer matches the scope.
Specification as shared reference The specification describes what the system should do. It is the shared reference for intent, and code serves it. It can be wrong, so it is reviewed, corrected and maintained. Implementation detail becomes outdated when the code is refactored.
Current-state knowledge The project describes the capabilities and behaviour it has today, not only the work it plans. Behaviour changes, but the description does not.
Change as a first-class unit A modification has its own record: why it is needed, what changes, how it will be built and how the result is checked. Later decisions are made in code and are not recorded.
Separation of current and proposed state The team can tell what the system does today apart from what a proposed change adds, modifies or removes. Proposed changes are merged into the description before they are built.
Shared project context Conventions, constraints, architectural rules and quality expectations are available to every contributor and every AI session. Conventions are not reviewed again, and agents follow outdated rules.
Traceability Requirements are linked to the design, tasks, tests and code that implement them. Links become outdated when code or tests move.
Reviewability Intent and plan can be reviewed before code is written, not only afterward. Review happens after the code exists. The reviewer rebuilds the intent from the diff.
Validation Acceptance criteria and tests decide whether the implementation fulfils the specification. Tests check the expectations that were written down, not every goal.
Living documentation After a change is completed, the specification is updated so future work starts from an accurate picture. Updates are skipped. The next change is planned against outdated text.
Human control Humans decide what to build, review trade-offs, approve changes and remain accountable for the result. Approval loses its force when the one who judges the work also produced it.

These cornerstones are not bureaucratic overhead. They are mechanisms that preserve context. AI needs this context. Teams have always needed it too, but they often kept it in informal conversations. A team that keeps the cornerstones in place does not add ceremony for its own sake. It reduces the number of things that people have to remember or guess.

2.5 Problems SDD solves

SDD is most effective where context is missing, temporary or inconsistent. Chapter 1 showed ambiguity, lost context, drift and weak review in detail. Four more consequences follow from the same gap:

  • Inconsistent AI output. Shared conventions and constraints help agents produce results that fit the project, so that an agent does not invent a new pattern in every session.
  • Poor onboarding. A new developer or agent can read the current specifications to understand the major capabilities and constraints. This reading is worth most where specifications pass between developers and other roles. In a team of developers only, it adds a document to read, and it changes less than the argument suggests.
  • Unclear scope. Explicit requirements and exclusions make trade-offs visible. Without anyone noticing, chapter 1's CSV export request can gain a filter, a permission rule and a size limit that nobody asked for.
  • Fragmented knowledge. Requirements, rationale, tasks and validation criteria are connected, and not scattered across chats, tickets, wikis and comments.

These are problems of communication and memory, not of coding skill. SDD improves the record, not the ability to write code. A team that cannot write a clear requirement does not become able to write one by adopting a framework. The framework only makes the gap visible sooner.

2.6 Problems SDD does not solve

SDD does not solve every problem. It improves the quality of communication and decision-making. But it cannot replace the responsibilities of software engineering.

  • It does not guarantee correct requirements. A precise specification of the wrong behaviour is still wrong.
  • It does not remove the need for testing. Specifications define expected behaviour. Tests and verification still prove that the implementation behaves as intended.
  • It does not make a passing result independent. Tests are often written by the same agent as the code, from the same reading of the requirement. So a passing run can confirm a misunderstanding that the tests and the code share.
  • It does not remove architectural judgment. Choosing between designs, weighing trade-offs and understanding long-term consequences are still human work.
  • It does not make bad product decisions good. SDD can make a decision clearer. It cannot decide business value, priorities or user needs by itself.
  • It does not remove the need for code review. Generated code still needs inspection for correctness, security, performance, maintainability and fit with the system.
  • It does not make every task worth specifying. Chapter 1 discussed how to judge when the cost is worth it. This list is about the limits that remain even then.
  • It does not automatically stop specifications from decaying. Specifications must be maintained, or they become misleading documentation.

The limits are the limits of any written record, not a defect in the idea. A record can be precise and still describe the wrong thing. Even a well-judged record cannot decide what is worth building. It also cannot replace the judgment that keeps it accurate.

Decay has a mechanism. That mechanism is the reason the cornerstone asks for what rather than how. Implementation detail helps an agent that lacks context. It also makes the record outdated as soon as the code changes. A named class, function or library version changes when the code is refactored, while the behaviour it produces does not. Well-structured detail improves what an agent produces, so the answer is not less detail. The answer is to keep the detail apart from the behaviour it serves, and to expect the detail to be replaced.

A passing test is a weak signal on its own. It can pass because the work is right, or because the test never checks the claim. The result looks the same in both cases. Evidence requires the possibility of failure. Only a test that could have failed shows anything about the claim. Confirmation proves little. A failed expectation is what shows that the test was looking at the claim.

A requirement that constrains a state does not say how a transition between two states is carried out. The design records that decision. It also records why it chose one order over another.

2.7 Why developers remain essential

AI changes the daily work of developers, but it does not remove the need for them. Developers translate incomplete human goals into precise, testable intent. They understand the organization around the system, evaluate risk and take responsibility for what is delivered. A model can produce an implementation. It cannot decide what should exist, why it should exist, or whether the result is acceptable.

In an SDD way of working, developers spend more time on activities that require judgment:

  • understanding user and business problems;
  • identifying constraints, risks and non-functional requirements;
  • designing and reviewing architectural options;
  • writing and reviewing specifications;
  • questioning AI-generated plans and implementations;
  • reviewing security, privacy, performance and maintainability;
  • deciding what should be automated and what should remain manual;
  • maintaining a coherent system rather than a collection of isolated generated fragments.

The developer's role shifts from typing every line to directing, reviewing and integrating work. That is a change in emphasis, not a loss of relevance. AI can make implementation faster, but humans remain responsible for deciding what should exist, why, and whether the result is acceptable.

Whoever writes a record pays its cost. Its benefit goes to people who come later. So a team must decide which work deserves a record.

SDD is best understood as a contract between the people who want a system, the people who build it and the AI tools that help build it. It makes intent explicit, keeps that intent available and connects it to implementation and verification. That is what stops the model from guessing and the team from relying on memory. The cornerstones are the terms of that contract. They name what must be preserved, what must be reviewed and what remains human responsibility. Something still has to carry those terms. The next chapter shows one implementation that carries them, and what the conventions cannot carry.

3. How OpenSpec Carries the Cornerstones

Chapter 1 introduced OpenSpec as one example of a spec-driven way of working, and it named the artifacts of OpenSpec only in passing. Chapter 2 named the principles that those artifacts have to satisfy. This chapter shows how one set of conventions implements those principles. It also shows where the conventions stop.

This chapter is a map, not a manual. One section gives the technical background, for the reader who wants to know what the conventions run on. Installation, commands and configuration belong to the tool's own documentation. What matters here is the shape of the record. Where is intent written down? How is a proposed change kept apart from the system as it is? What keeps the two connected? A different tool could arrange the same material under other names and still serve the same principles. So the question to keep in mind through the chapter is not what the tool does. It is which principle each convention serves.

3.1 What the tool consists of

OpenSpec is a small program, not a platform. It is an open-source command-line tool under the MIT license, maintained by Fission-AI and written in TypeScript. It is distributed as an npm package, or as a standalone binary that runs without Node.js. A developer installs it once on a machine and uses it per project. There is no service to sign up for and nothing to host. The OpenSpec project plans its own development with OpenSpec, so its repository is a working example of the conventions this chapter describes.

All of a project's artifacts are Markdown files in the repository. There is no server, no daemon, no database and no API key. Nothing that the work depends on runs between commands. What the project plans and specifies is in Markdown files and nowhere else. The program does keep some state on the machine: the global configuration with its profile, schemas that a user shares across projects, skills installed for every project, and stores registered as standalone OpenSpec repositories. It also sends anonymous usage statistics: the command's name and the release, and nothing of the project. It does not send them if OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 is set or the configuration turns them off. The openspec/ tree is plain files, and git versions and shares them like any other file. A session never depends on a service being reachable, because the work uses none. A project that stops using the tool keeps files that any editor can read. The format is Markdown, and the tool operates on it rather than containing it.

The work is split between the agent and the program. The agent in the coding tool drafts and edits the artifacts, because that part needs language and judgment. The program does what should not depend on a model. It parses the Markdown structure, checks the conventions, and counts task checkboxes to compute progress. It also refuses a change that fails validation. At archive, the merge of a delta into the main specifications has two paths. The openspec archive command makes the merge in the program. The archive workflow has the agent make the merge, following the rules of the sync workflow, and then validates the main specifications. A later chapter describes both paths. Reporting commands can produce machine-readable output, so the checks can run wherever checks belong. A model writes, a program verifies, and a person approves. A passing validation is a fact about structure, not a verdict on the requirements. The limits from chapter 2 apply unchanged. Structure is exactly the part that a program can be trusted with.

The tool connects to the coding tools through generated files, not through a protocol. The setup command, openspec init, writes the skills of OpenSpec into one shared directory, in whatever file format the coding tools expect. From release 2.1, that directory is by default ~/.agents/skills/, which every project on the machine shares. With --scope project, it is the repository's own .agents/skills/. The line skillsScope: project in the project's configuration then records that choice for everyone who clones the repository. This repository keeps its skills in the project. Each skill delivers one workflow, which is OpenSpec's word for one action on a change. A profile chooses which workflows are installed. A coding tool reads that directory, either directly or through links of its own. The current release writes no slash commands. The repository's README names the release that this description was checked against. The openspec update command generates those files again when the program changes. So the instructions an agent sees stay consistent with the program that checks the agent's work. No protocol stands between the program and the assistant: not an MCP server, and not an API. No assistant is privileged. What the connection moves is text, and text is the one thing that every coding tool already reads.

The shape of a change is data. A schema is a folder of plain files. One YAML file declares each artifact that a change produces: the file it generates, what it requires first, and the instruction the agent receives when it creates the artifact. There is also one Markdown template per artifact. A line in the project's configuration names the schema to use. The default schema produces the four artifacts this chapter describes: proposal, delta specifications, design and tasks. A project can fork a schema and edit it. It can drop an artifact, add one, or rewrite the instructions. The program then enforces the project's schema as if the schema had been shipped that way. The dependencies between artifacts are enablers, not phase gates. They say what becomes possible, not what must happen next. The project decides what a change folder contains, not the tool, and the tool checks whatever the project declared.

The nature of the tool is now stated: a program over plain Markdown versioned by git, which checks what agents write. What remains to describe is what those files hold.

3.2 The two parts of the record

The design is easier to remember when it is reduced to two locations in the repository. One set of specifications describes the system as it is today. A separate set of change folders describes work that is proposed or in progress. Both are in a directory called openspec/, next to the code they describe.

Everything else in this chapter follows from that split. If the specifications described only the work in progress, the project would have plans and no memory. If they described only the current system, a change would have no place to say what it intends. Because both are kept in one repository, a reader can ask two separate questions. What does this system do? And what is about to change?

3.3 The system as it is

The specifications under openspec/specs/ are organised by capability. A capability is a coherent area of behaviour, and each capability holds requirements and scenarios. A requirement states what must be true of the system. A scenario gives one concrete case that shows the requirement being met or missed.

This makes the cornerstone of current-state knowledge concrete. A developer or an agent who needs to know how the system behaves can read the capability. They do not have to reconstruct the behaviour from code, diagrams or memory. The specification is not a summary of the code, and it is not a design document. It states the behaviour that the code is supposed to have. For that reason, it can be used to judge the code, and not merely to describe it. That is what the convention asks for, but it is not what most repositories contain. Most specifications written this way carry implementation detail, and the detail is there because it helps the agent that reads it. The rule protects the part that has to outlive the code. That is the cornerstone of the specification as shared reference.

3.4 A change as a folder

A proposed modification is in openspec/changes/<change-name>/. The folder is self-contained. It holds the proposal, which explains why the work is needed, and the delta specifications, which state what changes. It also holds the design, which explains the approach, and the tasks, which break the work into steps. Chapter 1 named these artifacts. The point here is that they are in one place.

That grouping is the cornerstone of a change as a first-class unit, and it is also the cornerstone of reviewability. A reviewer can read the intent, the expected behaviour and the plan before any code exists. The reviewer does not have to reconstruct them from a diff. The grouping also makes a change a unit of work rather than a side effect of version control. A change can be reviewed, revised or abandoned without leaving a half-finished branch behind.

Chapter 1 used the request "add CSV export" to show how much a single sentence leaves undecided. The same request shows what a change folder has to hold. As a change, it becomes add-csv-export/. The folder has to answer the questions that the sentence left open: which records are exported, which columns, whether the current filter applies, how dates and numbers are formatted, and who is permitted to export what. The illustration is the one that chapter 1 used, not a change in this repository. Its value is that the request is small enough to remember while the conventions are introduced.

A delta specification does not repeat the whole system specification. It states only what the change does to that specification, using explicit operations: a requirement can be added, modified, removed or renamed. OpenSpec names the four operations ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED and RENAMED. So the kind of change is part of the record, and a reader does not have to infer it. The CSV export change adds a requirement that describes export. It may also modify a requirement about who may see which records, because exporting is one way of seeing them. The change leaves the rest of the capability alone.

As a result, the effect of a change on behaviour is visible in one place. A reviewer sees both the new behaviour and its effect on existing behaviour. The reviewer does not have to hold two versions of the whole specification side by side. This is the cornerstone of separation of current and proposed state, expressed as an operation rather than as advice about where to write things. The same record names what the change leaves alone. An exclusion that is written down is a decision, not a gap that a later reader has to guess at.

3.5 The rules that apply to all work

The repository also holds the rules that apply to every change: how the project is structured, which standards apply, and what must not break. These rules are in the instruction files that an agent reads when a session opens. One of them is AGENTS.md, which is also the one such file that several coding tools read. The rules are also in the project context that the tool loads before planning. Because those rules are kept with the code, the same material is available to a developer, a reviewer and an agent.

That is the cornerstone of shared project context. It does not mean that an agent reads the rules automatically. It means that the rules have a place where they can be found. It also means that a session which consults them starts from the project's conventions, and not from a generic default.

3.6 From intent to a merged specification

The artifacts form a path. The proposal says why the work is needed. This is explicit intent, written down before anything is built. The delta says what behaviour changes. The design says how the work will be approached. The tasks connect the design to implementation steps. Each artifact can be checked against the one before it. So a disagreement between intent and plan becomes visible before it becomes a disagreement between plan and code.

That path is the cornerstone of traceability, and it is short on purpose. A change does not have to fill every artifact to be traceable. But it has to be possible to follow the reasoning from the request to the code, without guessing which decision came from where.

A requirement is identified by its own title. The identifier goes with design decisions and tasks, and the specification holds the wording. Everything else points to the requirement. A chapter or an artifact that discusses what the requirement says uses the name, and leaves the sentence where it is. When the wording is copied along, a second copy of a rule appears in a document that is edited on a different schedule. Two copies of one rule can disagree.

Validation is the check at the end of the path. That check is the cornerstone of validation. Acceptance criteria and tests decide whether the implementation satisfies the specification. The specification is the reference for that decision, and the implementation is not its own judge. This is what stops a written record from becoming a description written after the fact. If the code decides what counts as correct, the specification records the outcome of the work. If the specification decides, the work can fail to meet it, and the failure is visible.

Completion keeps the record alive. When the work is finished, the delta is merged into the capability's specification, so the description of the system matches the system again. The change folder then moves into a dated archive. There it keeps the record of what changed and the design that went with it.

That is the cornerstone of living documentation. It is the difference between a specification written before coding and one that is maintained. The current specification is updated because the work changed, not because someone remembered to update it. The archive is not a backup. It is the record of how the current description reached its form. The reasoning in it is only as complete as the people who wrote the change made it. A decision that was settled in a conversation and never written into the change is not in the archive, and nothing later can recover it.

3.7 What the conventions leave to people

None of this decides what to build. The conventions give intent a place, a shape and a check, but they do not supply the intent. A change folder can hold a proposal that argues for the wrong feature. It can hold a delta that specifies the wrong behaviour, and tasks that implement it carefully. The record does not prevent that. It makes the decision visible, and that allows someone to challenge the decision before it is built.

That is the last cornerstone, human control, and it is the one that the conventions cannot carry. A tool can hold a decision. It cannot make one.

Validation happens at the end of the change, and nothing checks afterwards whether the specification and the code still agree. A later change can satisfy its own requirement and pass its own tests. It can still break a constraint from an earlier change without anyone noticing. No tool in the sample was shown to look for that. The practitioners who wanted such a check had to build checks of their own. A check would show a disagreement, but not which of the two is wrong.

Most people who work this way read a specification in part rather than in full, or pass the review to another agent. Partial reading is partly what the record is for. The problem, the decisions and the acceptance criteria carry the intent, and the rest is context for whoever implements. Passing the review to another agent is the risk, because it removes the one point at which a person decides what the system should do. The record does not help there either. It shows the path that was taken, and a rejected alternative survives only if someone wrote it down.

The conventions are worth reading as answers to the cornerstones, not as a directory layout. Ten of the eleven cornerstones have a convention in this chapter that carries them, and human control is the limit named above. The split between what the system is and what is about to change carries most of the principles. The rest are carried by where the material is kept, by the path from proposal to tasks, and by the fact that the work is checked against the specification rather than the code. The next chapter follows one requirement through this path, from a sentence that looks complete to the constraint that settles it.

4. One Change from Request to Archive

A customer pays 100 cents for a product that costs 70 cents. The machine owes the customer 30 cents. Written as a request, that sentence sounds complete. It does not say which coins the machine should use. It also does not say what happens when the machine has no coins left, or whether the product is given out before the change is counted. These questions must become artifacts before anyone writes code. This chapter follows one change on its path from the request to the archive. The example is small: a vending machine that gives change. The example is kept in its own repository, with its own OpenSpec root, and it contains no code. What the reader sees here is what the tool produces at each stage.

4.1 A change is a folder

In OpenSpec, a change is a folder under openspec/changes/, named after the change. The path from a request to an archived change has four stages, which the first table shows. The folder holds the artifacts that the path produces. The second table lists them, together with the other files of a change.

Stage What happens
Request The starting statement of what the change should do, as in the opening paragraph.
Create the artifacts The propose workflow creates the four artifacts listed in the second table, in the order that the schema declares. The specification and the design each need only the proposal, and the tasks need both of them. This order decides what can be made next; it is not a set of gates that must be passed in turn, as chapter 3 explains.
Validation The validate command checks the change's delta specifications. It also looks in the main specifications for the capabilities that the change says it will modify.
Archive Archiving merges the change's specification into the main specification. It also moves the change folder into the archive.

The artifacts come from spec-driven, the default schema of the tool.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Archive moves it into the archive. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Archive writes it. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows. It also holds skip_specs when the change has no deltas. Chapter 4

The two tables answer different questions. The first says what happens to a change over time. The second says what the change's folder holds. A reader who keeps the two apart will see that the tool's stages are not documents. The reader will also see that the documents are not a checklist of stages. Validation and archive are the only stages that add no file to the change. validate reads the delta. Archive writes the delta into the main specification and moves the change out of the working folder.

The example change is give-exact-change. It is in ../vending-machine, a separate repository with its own OpenSpec root. It adds a capability called purchase. Its first requirement is the one that this chapter follows to the end: the machine gives change in coins from its stock. A second change, refuse-without-exact-change, revises that requirement. Both changes are archived in the example repository. The quotations below are taken from them as they were written.

4.2 The proposal

The proposal is the first artifact. It says why the change exists and what it changes. It does not say how the work is done. That belongs to the design. The default template has four parts: Why, What Changes, Capabilities and Impact.

Proposal Description
Why The problem or opportunity in one or two sentences: why the change is needed. The first change gives two sentences.
What Changes A list of what is added, modified or removed. The first change adds the capability purchase with two requirements.
Capabilities The capabilities that the change creates or modifies, each with the spec file it needs. The first change creates purchase.
Impact The files, specifications or systems that the change affects. The first change names the spec file that archiving will create.

The proposal of the change give-exact-change is proposal.md. It is shown in full as archived:

## Why

A customer who pays more than the price of a product expects the difference back.
The machine holds coins, so it has to decide which coins make up the difference.

## What Changes

- Add a capability `purchase` with two requirements: the coins the machine holds,
  and the change it returns for a purchase.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities

- `purchase`: the coins the machine holds, and the change it returns for a purchase.

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — created when this change is archived.

4.3 The specification

The specification is the delta in the change's folder. It states what the system must do. Each requirement is a statement with SHALL, and each requirement has scenarios. A change does not rewrite the whole main specification. The main specification holds the requirements of the system as they now stand, at openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md. A delta says what the change adds, modifies or removes, and archive merges the delta later. The delta is written to specs/<capability>/spec.md in the change folder.

Specification Description
Purpose For a new capability: one or two sentences on what the capability is for. Archiving copies it into the main specification. The first delta has one.
ADDED / MODIFIED Requirements The operation that the delta performs on the requirements of the main specification. The first change adds two requirements, and the second change modifies one.
Requirement One statement of what the system must do, written with SHALL.
Scenario One case under a requirement. WHEN states the condition that can be set up, and THEN states the outcome that can be decided.

The first change uses ADDED, because the capability did not exist yet. Its delta is specs/purchase/spec.md in the change give-exact-change, shown in full as archived. It opens with a Purpose section. It holds two requirements, each with its scenarios:

## Purpose

Defines the coins the vending machine holds and the change it returns for a purchase, so that a customer who pays more than the price receives the difference in coins from the machine's stock.

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine holds coins of four denominations

The machine SHALL hold coins of 10, 20, 50 and 100 cents only. Amounts are stated in
cents.

#### Scenario: Stock holds only the four denominations

- **WHEN** the machine is stocked
- **THEN** every coin in its stock is a coin of 10, 20, 50 or 100 cents

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, in coins from its stock.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

This scenario can be set up with a stock of coins, and it says exactly which coins come back. The requirement alone does not say that, but the scenario does. The second change adds a third scenario of the same kind. The first version did not have it. It appears in section 4.8.

4.4 The design

The design is the third artifact. It records the decisions that the requirement leaves open, and the reason for each one. The requirement says what the machine returns. The design says in which order the machine works and how it finds the coins.

Design Description
Context The current state and the constraints that shape the approach. It does not restate the motivation, which is in the proposal. The first design's Context restates the requirement and says what the design covers.
Goals / Non-Goals What the design aims for, and what it leaves out at design level. The first design states one goal and two non-goals. One of its non-goals is the case in which section 4.7 shows the design failing.
Decisions Each decision with its reason, and the rejected alternative where there was one. The default template asks for "rationale and alternatives considered".
Risks / Trade-offs Each risk, followed by its mitigation. The first design names one risk: the stock of coins runs down, and refilling is left outside the change.

The first design's Context states the requirement that it serves and says what the design covers. Its goals and non-goals come next, then its decisions, and its risks come last. Each decision is laid out as a decision, a reason and, where one was rejected, an alternative. This layout is this project's own. The tool's template asks for decisions with rationale and alternatives, and it does not prescribe a layout. The design of give-exact-change is design.md. It is shown in full as archived, and it reads:

## Context

The purchase capability requires the machine to return the difference in coins from
its stock. This design says how the machine works out those coins and in what order
it does its steps.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the difference between the amount inserted and the price, in coins from the
  stock.

**Non-Goals:**

- Deciding what happens when the stock cannot make the change. This design does not
  say.
- Choosing the coins so that the stock stays balanced, or so that the fewest coins are
  returned.

## Decisions

**Decision**: release the product first, then work out the change from the coins in
stock.

**Why**: the customer should not wait at the machine after the payment is complete.

**Decision**: work out the change greedily. Take the largest coin that does not
exceed the amount still owed, for as long as the stock of that coin lasts. Repeat
until nothing is owed.

**Why**: the method is short to state and easy to trace by hand.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- The stock of coins shrinks with each purchase, and nothing in this design refills it.
  → Refilling is outside this change; the design assumes a stocked machine.

## Findings

Each scenario is traced through the design by hand.

- **Scenario "Change is given from stock"**: 100 inserted, 70 price, 30 owed. The
  largest coin that does not exceed 30 is 20; one is returned, 10 is owed. The
  largest coin that does not exceed 10 is 10; one is returned, nothing is owed.
  Result: 20 and 10. Matches the scenario.
- **Scenario "Exact payment gives no change"**: 70 inserted, 70 price, nothing owed.
  No coin is returned. Result: none. Matches the scenario.

The first design records no rejected alternative. The rest of the chapter depends on its two decisions.

The file does not end with its risks. It ends with a Findings section, and the template's design has no such part. The template's parts are Context, Goals / Non-Goals, Decisions and Risks / Trade-offs. The example keeps the section as a stated exception. The walkthroughs must be written down somewhere. Next to the decisions they test, they are read by anyone who reads the decisions. The cost of the exception is that the chapter must keep the section true, because no part of the tool checks it.

4.5 The tasks

The tasks are the last artifact. They turn the design into checks, one for each part of the design that must be verified. Each task is a checkbox, and the tool counts the checkboxes to show progress.

Tasks Description
Group heading A numbered heading that groups related tasks. The first change has one group, "Check the first version".
Task A checkbox with a number and a description of the check. [ ] is open and [x] is done.
Verified by A clause after the task that names the evidence that the check passed. The example's own rules fix the wording of the clause. The default instruction asks each task to state how it is verified, and the template has no part for it.

The tasks of give-exact-change are tasks.md, shown in full as archived. They name three checks under one group heading. The first two of them trace a scenario through the design:

## 1. Check the first version

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario "Exact payment gives no change" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

The first two tasks send the reader to the Findings section of the design quoted in section 4.4. The trace that each task names is there. The third task records validation. Validation passed the first version. The validate command reads the change's delta specifications. It reads the main specifications only to see what the delta modifies. It does not read the proposal, the design or the tasks of a change that has not been archived. It does not check whether the design agrees with the scenarios, and chapter 3 names that limit. Here the limit has a concrete consequence. The first change was complete by every check that the tool runs. Still, the design did not satisfy a case that had not yet been written down.

A task list is easy to read as a plan of work. The tasks in this example are checks. Ticking one records that the check was made, not only that someone intended to make it. That difference matters later, when the box is the only record of what was done.

4.6 Archiving the first change

Archiving closes a change. Until then, the change is a set of artifacts that describe a behaviour the system does not have yet. After archiving, the change folder is kept as a record, and the behaviour it describes is part of the main specification. Archiving is done in one run, but it decides what the next change is checked against. For this reason, it is shown here on its own.

The first change is ready for archiving when two things hold. First, its tasks are checked and validation passes: task 1.3 records the validation command passing. Second, its design's Findings trace both of its scenarios. So the design and the scenarios agree on the cases that existed when the change was written.

For a new capability, archiving does four things. First, it creates the main specification for the capability, openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md. Second, it copies the delta's Purpose into that file. This is why the delta begins with a Purpose section. Without one, the new file holds a placeholder that someone must replace by hand. Third, it writes the delta's requirements into the file. Fourth, it moves the change folder into the archive, under its date. The folder is kept as a record, but it is no longer work in progress. The first lines of openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md, as give-exact-change left them when it was archived, read:

# purchase Specification

## Purpose
Defines the coins the vending machine holds and the change it returns for a purchase, so that a customer who pays more than the price receives the difference in coins from the machine's stock.

## Requirements

### Requirement: The machine holds coins of four denominations

The machine SHALL hold coins of 10, 20, 50 and 100 cents only. Amounts are stated in
cents.

The example was archived with OpenSpec 2.0.0. From release 2.1.1, archive also leaves a blank line after the ## Purpose heading, and the file says the same. The file has a title, a Purpose and the requirements of the first change, and nothing else. It does not name the change that wrote it. That record is the archived folder, which holds the proposal, the design, the tasks and the delta. The main specification says what the system is. The archive says how it came to be.

Archiving does not decide whether the change is right. The tasks and the walkthrough of the scenarios decided that earlier. Archiving records a decision that has already been made, and it does so only when the change is closed. This is why the first change is archived before the second one begins. The second change modifies a requirement that exists in the main specification only after the archive.

4.7 The case that nobody had written

The second change, refuse-without-exact-change, starts from the main specification that section 4.6 created. It modifies one of that file's requirements, so it can be written only after the first change is closed. Its archive is in section 4.14. It starts from a case that the first version lacked. The requirement says that the machine returns the difference in coins from its stock. So the question is what happens when the stock cannot make that difference. In the case, the stock holds one coin of 10 cents and no coin of 20 or 50 cents. When the case is traced through the first design, it fails. The design had named this case as a non-goal, so it never decided it. The design releases the product, returns 10 of the 30 cents owed, and cannot return the remaining 20. The walkthrough is recorded in the Findings of design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, labelled Trace A. It reads:

**Trace A: the first design, scenario "Stock cannot make the change".** The price is
70, 100 is inserted, so 30 is owed. The stock holds one coin of 10 and none of 20.
The first design releases the product first. The largest coin that does not exceed 30
is 10, so one is returned and 20 is still owed. No coin can be returned for 20. The
customer leaves with the product and 10 of the 30 owed, and nothing says so.

The walkthrough shows two symptoms. The product is released before the change is worked out. The change returned is less than the amount owed, and there is no sign of it.

4.8 The correction

This section describes the second change, refuse-without-exact-change. It is a separate change, with its own folder and its own artifacts, and it does not edit the first change. The first change was archived in section 4.6, before the second one began. Its requirement was in the main specification, and its design was not reopened.

The second change starts where section 4.7 ends. Its proposal gives the reason in its Why section, which says three things. The first version has no answer for a stock that cannot make the change. The walkthrough of the scenario shows two symptoms. Validation had passed the first version anyway. The design of the second change says that it replaces the order of steps of the first design. It also records the walkthrough that shows why.

The second change does three things, and each one is in a different artifact:

  • Its proposal changes the requirement. The machine must return the exact amount. If it cannot, it refuses the purchase, releases no product and returns the amount inserted.
  • Its specification adds a scenario for a stock that cannot make the change.
  • Its design works out the change before the product is released.

Each of the four files of the second change has its own section below. The sections follow the order that the schema declares: the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks. Each section follows the pattern of the matching section for the first change, so that the two can be read side by side. Section 4.13 compares the two changes.

4.9 The proposal of the second change

The proposal of the second change answers a different question from the first proposal. The first proposal says why a customer should receive change at all. This one says why a rule that the first change wrote must be changed. Its reason is a walkthrough, not a situation. The four parts are the same, and each part is filled from that reason.

Second change: proposal What this change puts there
Why The failure that the walkthrough found: two symptoms, and the fact that validation passed the first version anyway.
What Changes Three changes. The requirement requires exact change, a scenario is added for a stock that cannot make the change, and the design works out the change before release.
Capabilities One modified capability, purchase, and the requirement it changes. No capability is created.
Impact The main specification that the first change created. This change modifies that file when it is archived.

refuse-without-exact-change, proposal.md

## Why

While writing the scenario for a stock that cannot make the change, the first version
has no answer. Tracing the scenario through the design of `give-exact-change` shows two
symptoms:

1. The product is released before the change is worked out. A customer who is short
   of change keeps the product.
2. With short stock the change is less than the amount owed, and nothing says so.

`openspec validate` passed the first version. It checks the structure of the
artifacts, not whether a design agrees with a scenario.

## What Changes

- The requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" requires exact
  change. If the exact change cannot be made, the purchase is refused and the amount
  inserted is returned. No product is released.
- A scenario is added for a stock that cannot make the change.
- The design works out the change before the product is released.

## Capabilities

### Modified Capabilities

- `purchase`: the requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" changes to require exact change.

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — the change requirement is modified when this
  change is archived.

The Why section differs most from the first proposal's Why. The first contains no reference to any file. The second cites one: the design of give-exact-change, which is the artifact that the walkthrough tested. So a reader can check the reason by following the trace in section 4.7. The first proposal could not have been written in this form, because the failure was not known until the walkthrough had been made.

The Capabilities section uses the Modified heading. Under that heading, the template asks for the exact path of an existing specification. So the delta must match a file that already exists. The first change created its capability and used the New heading, which had no such constraint.

Impact names the main specification and no new file. The first change's Impact named the file that archiving would create. This one names the file that archiving will change. Neither proposal has a Non-goals part, because the example removed it: the default template does not have one.

4.10 The specification of the second change

A delta for a modified capability has one job: it replaces a requirement in a specification that already exists. So it holds the whole requirement. It holds no Purpose, because the specification that it changes already has one. The tool ignores a Purpose in such a delta. The first delta began with a Purpose because it created a capability. This one begins with the requirement.

Second change: specification What this change puts there
MODIFIED Requirements One requirement, under a MODIFIED heading. The delta replaces the existing requirement of that name.
Requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock", written out in full. It gains the word "exactly" and a second sentence about refusal.
Scenario Three scenarios. The first two keep the text they had in the first change. The third is added here.
Purpose Not present. The main specification keeps the Purpose it already has.

refuse-without-exact-change, specs/purchase/spec.md

## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, exactly, in coins from its stock. If it cannot return
that exact amount, it SHALL refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the
amount inserted.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

#### Scenario: Stock cannot make the change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds one coin
  of 10 cents and no coin of 20 or 50 cents
- **THEN** the machine refuses the purchase, releases no product, and returns the 100
  cents inserted

Compare the first sentence of the requirement with the first change's version. One word has been inserted: "exactly". The sentence after it is new. It states the outcome that the first requirement left open. The scenario is the only place where that outcome can be decided as a case.

The two earlier scenarios keep their text. So the requirement is now checked against those two cases and the new one. The new scenario uses the same price and the same coin inserted as the first scenario, but a different stock. The first scenario needs at least one coin of 20 cents. The new one needs no coin of 20 or 50 cents. The two cases divide the stock by the 20-cent coin, although they do not cover every stock.

The schema warns that a MODIFIED delta with partial content loses detail when it is archived. So the requirement is quoted whole, as the replacement that archiving writes into the main specification.

4.11 The design of the second change

The design of the second change explains the requirement's new outcome, not only the order of steps. It is the file that replaces the first design's order. It records the alternatives that were rejected. It also records the walkthrough that shows the new order works for the case that failed.

Second change: design What this change puts there
Context Names the first design by its change, and says that this design replaces its order of steps.
Goals / Non-Goals One goal: exact change, or refusal with the amount inserted returned. Two non-goals: the coin denominations and any message to the customer.
Decisions Two decisions, each with a reason, and two rejected alternatives. The first design recorded no alternative.
Risks / Trade-offs One risk: refusals become more likely as the stock runs down. The design leaves the mitigation outside the change.
Findings Traces B, C and D for the revised design, and Trace A for the first. Not a template part. The example keeps it as a stated exception, explained in section 4.4.

refuse-without-exact-change, design.md

## Context

The design of `give-exact-change` released the product first and then worked out the
change greedily from the stock. Its findings traced the first two scenarios correctly.
The scenario "Stock cannot make the change" was not traced then, because it did not
exist. This design replaces the order of steps and records the trace that shows why.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the exact difference in coins from the stock, or refuse the purchase and return
  the amount inserted.

**Non-Goals:**

- Changing the coin denominations.
- Telling the customer why a purchase was refused.

## Decisions

**Decision**: work out the change before the product is released.

**Why**: the requirement says the change is exact. A product that is released before
the change is known cannot be taken back, so the exactness of the change must be
decided first.

**Decision**: if the greedy method does not reach the exact amount, refuse the
