The design, with the tasks written from it Those too, because the tasks were written from the decisions that changed.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. A later gap goes into a new change. The design of that change names, in its Context, the design it replaces.

The archive keeps the decisions as they were made. Section 5.9 says this of the proposal, and the same reason applies here. The example shows the bottom row and not the middle one. The second change's design is a new design in a new change. It names the first design in its Context, replaces the order of steps, and traces all three scenarios again, as section 4.11 shows. The first design is not touched. The middle row, a design revised while its tasks exist, has no case in the archive. Chapter 5 gives the reason: the second change was written after the first was archived, from a finding.

A revision can be made in two ways. The developer can edit the file, or the developer can ask the agent to change it. The choice depends on whether the replacement is known. The developer edits when the decision is already worked out. The developer asks the agent when the decision has to be worked out from the delta and the other decisions. The table compares the two ways on four points.

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is known, and the fault is in one decision or one reason The decision has to be worked out from the delta, the other decisions or the traces
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one change A request with three parts, a whole file to read again, and a diff so large that it hides what changed
How it goes wrong An edit to one decision leaves its goal, its risk or its trace no longer consistent with it A request for a clearer decision returns a rewrite that changes what was decided
What to check afterwards The goals, risks and traces that the decision touches The whole file, including the decisions that nobody meant to change

Suppose that the second reason of the first design had said that the method is the usual one. The developer knows the sentence that the archive holds: the method is short to state and easy to trace by hand. One sentence changes. Nothing else needs to change, because the wording of a reason is not an input to any trace. The diff shows that sentence and nothing else.

Suppose instead that a design, not one of the example's, records one decision with no alternative. The developer cannot yet say what was open. The request to the agent names that decision. It says that no alternative is recorded for it. It also says that the decision's text, its reason, the other decisions and the traces must not change. The agent proposes alternatives from the delta and the design's other decisions. The developer decides which of them anyone would have chosen. Without the third part, the agent may rewrite the whole Decisions part. The rewrite may change decisions that nobody asked about.

Both ways end in the same reading. An edit is checked by its diff. A revision made by asking the agent is a rewrite. So the whole design is read again as a new draft, using the four passes of section 7.8. Chapter 6 said that the tool catches a scenario dropped from a MODIFIED block. It does not catch a scenario whose text changed. A design has no such check. A decision can be dropped, or its reason changed, and validate still passes, because it never opens the file. The trace is what notices. It notices only for the scenarios that exist.

7.10 What the design passes on

The design passes to the tasks the decisions to check and the traces that have been done. The tasks are written from the design. Section 4.5 shows the first two tasks of the example, which are traces of its two scenarios. The design also passes on any open question. The instruction for the tasks asks for such a question to be resolved before the tasks are written. What the delta passed to the design, the design now holds as decisions. Each decision has its reason and, where an alternative was open, that alternative.

The tasks do not say what the system must do, and they do not decide how it works. They say how each decision is checked. They turn those checks into items that can be marked done. A command and a workflow that are not files close the change: validate and archive. Chapter 8 discusses the tasks and outlines what follows them. Chapters 11 and 12 describe them in full.

A design is the decisions that meet the cases. An agent drafts it. A program reads none of it. A person judges it by tracing the cases through it. The agent supplies the four parts and the form that the instruction asks for. The developer decides whether a design is needed and whether each reason holds. The tool checks none of the four parts, so the review is the whole of the check. A reason that can be compared with a requirement can be checked. A reason that is only convenience cannot. A non-goal is a statement that the review reads against the scenarios. A trace is the pass that finds a decision in conflict with a case. The reader should remember that a design is judged by two things: whether its scenarios can be traced through it, and whether what it leaves out is honest. A design that the tool accepts can still leave a scenario untraced, and finding that scenario is the reviewer's work.

8. The Tasks and the Evidence That a Check Was Made

Chapter 7 ended when the decisions and the traces were passed to the next artifact. That chapter said that this artifact says how each decision is checked. This chapter discusses that artifact and asks it the same four questions. Who writes it? Which of its parts must be right? How does a reviewer decide that it is finished? What happens when the review finds something wrong? The example is the same vending machine with the same two changes. Three things come after the tasks: the apply and archive workflows and the validate command. The end of this chapter gives them an outline, and chapters 11 and 12 describe them in full.

The table shows the files of a change and the paths of its specifications. The row this chapter discusses is in bold.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Archive moves it into the archive. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Archive writes it. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows. It also holds skip_specs when the change has no deltas. Chapter 4

The table lists the parts of tasks.md. The parts this chapter quotes or discusses are in bold.

Tasks Description
Group heading A numbered heading that groups related tasks.
Task A checkbox with a number and a description of the check. [ ] is open and [x] is done.

8.1 Who writes the tasks

The agent drafts the first version of tasks.md from the delta and the design. The tool lists these two artifacts as the dependencies of the tasks. Before the agent writes, the instruction tells it to read the design's Open Questions. It must resolve with the user any question that would change what gets built, so that no unstated assumption is built into the list. The agent supplies the form of the template, a task for each decision that seems sound, and a way to verify each task. The agent cannot supply what the team can really verify. It cannot say which evidence could fail, or what size of check fits one session. The developer's part is to ask of each task what would show that it had failed. Section 5.1 describes the same division for the proposal, and sections 6.1 and 7.1 describe it for the delta and the design. Chapter 2 gives the reason why human control stays with the developer.

In the spec-driven schema the tasks require both the delta and the design. So openspec status shows the tasks as blocked until both exist. The apply workflow, in turn, requires the tasks. The instruction of the apply workflow tells the agent to work through the pending tasks and to mark each one complete as it goes. In the default schema, therefore, the agent writes the check and also ticks it, and nothing records which of the two it did. Only a person can tell the check apart from the tick. The rest of this chapter is about how.

8.2 The parts of the tasks

The table says what the tool checks in each part of the tasks. For this artifact, the answer is a count.

Part What the tool checks The question it answers
Group heading Nothing. Which checks belong together, and in what order?
Task list, instructions apply and archive count the checkbox lines. A box holding only x or X is done. What has to be checked, and has it been checked?

The tool counts the content of the tasks, and of no other artifact, and it counts nothing but checkboxes. validate never opens the tasks.md of a change that has not been archived. Only the form --archived opens a tasks.md. It reads the tasks of archived changes and reports an open box as an error, as chapter 11 shows. status counts the file as done if it exists, whatever it contains. A file of one character, a file of prose and an empty file all show as done. list shows a file with no checkbox as "No tasks". instructions apply calls that change blocked. archive continues, because there is nothing to count. A box holding x, X or x is done. The markers [~], [-] and [] read as unfinished and are still counted. A line with no checkbox is not counted. The "1.1" in a task is text. instructions apply numbers the tasks by their position in the file, and a group heading does not appear in its output. The two parts are the whole of the default template. A part that a project adds belongs in a forked schema, as chapter 3 described. The tool therefore reads a number, and the number says how many boxes are ticked. It does not say whether any check was made. That is the finding of this section.

8.3 Groups and tasks

The file is tasks.md in the change give-exact-change. It is shown in full as archived:

## 1. Check the first version

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario "Exact payment gives no change" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

Its single group, "Check the first version", holds three tasks: two traces and a validation run. Each task is one check, and each box is ticked. The numbers 1.1 to 1.3 are the author's, as the previous section said. The tool does not read them.

The file is tasks.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change. It is shown in full as archived:

## 1. Trace the first version

- [x] 1.1 Write the scenario "Stock cannot make the change" from the requirement's word "exact". **Verified by** the scenario in the spec delta.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario through the first design of `give-exact-change`. **Verified by** Trace A in the design's Findings, which records both symptoms.

## 2. Revise and trace again

- [x] 2.1 Revise the design so that the change is worked out before release, and a change that is not exact is refused. **Verified by** the decisions in the design.
- [x] 2.2 Trace all three scenarios through the revised design. **Verified by** Traces B, C and D in the design's Findings.
- [x] 2.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

The second change has five tasks in two groups. In the first group, the failure is written down and traced. In the second group, the design is revised and checked again. So the second group cannot begin before the first group has given an answer. The instruction asks that the tasks be ordered by dependency and be small enough to finish in one session. Both files meet that: each task is one check. Section 4.12 says what the groups do.

Every box in both files is ticked, and the archive keeps them. A tick does not hold its evidence. Each task points at the delta, at a trace in the design's Findings, at the decisions or at a command. So the box is a pointer, and the file it names holds what it points at. A reader of the tasks alone learns that someone ticked. To learn why, the reader has to open the file that the task names. Section 4.5 says what a tick records. This chapter asks what a reader can do with one.

8.4 What the template leaves out

The instruction for the tasks asks for two things that the template does not have. The first is a statement in each task of how the task is verified. The instruction says that each task must state how to verify completion: with a test, a command, an observable behaviour or a delivered artifact. It says that this statement goes in the task's own description. The template has two checkbox placeholders and no part for the statement. The example fixes its wording through a rule in its project configuration, which asks each task to state how it is verified. Verified by is the example's wording of what the instruction already asks.

The file is tasks.md in the change give-exact-change. Its task 1.1 reads as archived:

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.

The evidence is a trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario. A reviewer opens the design, reads the trace and compares it with the scenario. The trace could have disagreed with the scenario, and the reviewer can see whether it did. Section 4.7 shows a trace of this kind.

The file is tasks.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change. Its task 2.1 reads as archived:

- [x] 2.1 Revise the design so that the change is worked out before release, and a change that is not exact is refused. **Verified by** the decisions in the design.

The evidence is the decisions in the design. The decision is both what was done and the proof that it was done. So this evidence cannot show a failure of its own. The question a reviewer asks of any task is whether its evidence could have come out the other way. Task 2.2 of the same file traces all three scenarios through the revised design. It is the task whose evidence can fail. The example shows both kinds next to each other, as written.

The example has three kinds of evidence. A reading, such as a trace in the design or a scenario in the delta, can be opened by someone who was not there. The work itself, such as the decisions of task 2.1, is the claim again. A command's result is the third kind. The last task of each file runs openspec validate --strict and names the command passing. That result is recorded by the box and by the clause, and nowhere else unless the task says where. validate, run on a change that has not been archived, reads the delta and never the design or the tasks, as sections 7.2 and 4.5 say. So those two tasks are evidence about the delta and no more. Section 4.5 says what followed for the first change.

The instruction's second addition is for steps that need the archive. It asks that the tracked tasks be work that can be completed before the archive. Any step that waits for the archive must be a plain bullet under an optional ## Workflow follow-up section, where the tool does not count it. The reason is in what archive does with an open box: it asks whether to continue. A box for the archive itself could not be ticked before the archive ran. So it would be an open box at the moment the archive counts. The instruction names the section for use when it applies, and neither example file has one.

8.5 Reviewing the tasks

The tasks are reviewed twice. The first review is made after the design is reviewed and before apply begins. It asks whether the checks are the right ones. The second review is made when the boxes are ticked. It reads each ticked box against the evidence that its task names. The tool shows the count at both moments and checks neither review. The review has four passes. Intent asks whether the tasks check this change and not another. Coverage asks whether each decision of the design, and each trace that the design passes on, has a task that checks it. It also asks whether each task checks something the design holds. Evidence asks whether each task's evidence could have come out the other way, and whether someone who was not there can open it. Order asks whether the tasks are small and ordered by dependency. It also asks whether they are grouped so that each group delivers its own tests and documentation. Coverage and evidence matter most, because the tool counts boxes and sees neither.

When every box is ticked, instructions apply reports the change as all done. It tells the agent to review or verify the change as appropriate before archiving. The tool leaves the verification to a person. The count says how many boxes are ticked. It does not say how many checks were made. The second review is the one that the count cannot do. It reads each ticked box in the file that its task names, and it finds the box whose evidence is absent.

The table is one checklist, in the order the file is read. The column names use the artifact's name, which here is the tasks.

Check The tasks pass when How a draft can fail
The request is answered as meant The tasks check the change that the design describes, and nothing in them answers an assumption the agent made The list checks another change, or adds work that the design does not hold
Group heading Each group names one part of the work, and the groups follow the order of the dependencies in the work A group collects checks of different kinds, or a final group holds tests or documentation that an earlier group owed
Task: size Each task is one check that can be finished in one session One task holds several checks under one box, so one tick stands for several claims
Task: coverage Each decision of the design, and each trace the design passes on, has a task that checks it. Each task checks something the design holds A decision has no task, so nothing checks it, or a task checks something that no decision states
Verification: statement Each task says how it is verified, in the form the instruction asks for A task names no evidence, or names only the work itself as evidence
Verification: evidence The evidence could have come out the other way, and someone who was not there can open it The evidence is the claim itself, or it is where no one can find it
Box Each ticked box has its evidence in the place the task names, and each open box has none yet A box is ticked and its evidence is absent, or the task was reworded after the tick
Workflow follow-up A step that waits for the archive is a plain bullet and not a box An archive step is written as a box, so the list cannot be finished before the archive it waits for
Downstream The count is complete because each task is ticked with its evidence, and the change can go to archive The list reads complete because an open task was removed or reworded, or an open box is left for the archive to ask about

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A row that passes records a person's judgement, not a machine's check. Three rows look beyond the file to the files its tasks name: the rows on evidence, on the box and on what is downstream. They are the rows that cannot be read from the tasks alone. A list whose count is complete and whose evidence cannot be opened is not finished. A task list is finished when each tick can be traced to its evidence, not when the count is complete.

8.6 Changing the tasks after review

When the review finds a fault, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first decision depends on how many boxes are ticked and on whether the change is archived.

What exists What the revision covers
Only the tasks, and no box ticked The task, its order and the tasks that depend on it.
The tasks, with boxes ticked Those too. A tick belongs to the task as it was, so a task whose wording changes is reopened until its check is made again.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. A later gap goes into a new change, whose tasks name the change they check.

The archive keeps the tasks as they were, as section 5.9 says of the proposal, and the same reason applies here. The example shows the bottom row and not the middle one. The second change's tasks are a new list in a new change. Its task 1.2 traces the design of the first change. The first change's list is untouched, and every box in it is still ticked. The middle row, a list revised while boxes are ticked, has no case in the archive. The reason is the one chapter 5 gives: the second change was written after the first was archived, from a finding.

A revision is made by editing the file or by asking the agent to change it. The choice depends on whether the replacement is known. The developer edits when the sentence is already known. The developer asks the agent when the check has to be worked out from the design, or when several tasks have to move together. The table compares the two ways on four points.

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is known, and the fault is in one task The check has to be worked out from the design, or several tasks have to move together
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one line A request with three parts, a whole file to read back, and a diff whose size hides what changed
How it goes wrong An edit changes what a task checks while its box stays ticked A request for a clearer list returns a renumbered one, in which boxes have changed state and the count has changed
What to check afterwards The task's box against its new wording, and the tasks that depend on it Each box against its evidence, and the whole list with its count

Suppose the first change's task 1.2 had named the first scenario, "Change is given from stock". The developer knows the name that the archive holds: "Exact payment gives no change". One name changes. The box was ticked against the trace of the first scenario. So the developer reads the trace that the task now names before the box stays ticked. The diff shows one name. The tick is the part that the diff does not show.

Suppose a task list, not one of the example's, holds a task whose evidence is "the design". The developer cannot yet say what would fail. The request to the agent has three parts:

  1. which task to revise: the one whose evidence is the design;
  2. what is wrong with it: the evidence cannot fail, because it is the work itself;
  3. what must not move: the other tasks, their order and the boxes already ticked.

The agent proposes evidence from the delta's scenarios and the design's traces. The developer decides which of them would catch a wrong design. Without the third part, the agent may renumber the list and change the state of boxes.

Both ways end in the same reading. An edit is checked by its diff, which includes the state of each box. A revision made by asking is a rewrite. So the whole list is read again as a new draft, with the passes of section 8.5 and with each box read against its evidence. Chapter 6 said that the tool reports a scenario dropped from a MODIFIED block. Chapter 7 said that the tool notices nothing in a design. The tasks are between these two cases. The count changes. A box that changed state and an open task that was removed both make the list read complete, in the same words. The tool is not wrong to count. It counts what it can see.

8.7 What the tasks pass on

The tasks are the one artifact that the next workflow reads, and the schema names them as the file that apply tracks. Three things follow the tasks: the apply workflow, the validate command and the archive workflow. This section gives each of them a paragraph. Each paragraph says what one of them does with the tasks, and gives one fact that a reader would not guess. Chapter 11 describes apply and the validate command, and chapter 12 describes archive, each with its own review and update guidance.

Apply is the workflow in which the boxes change. The agent works through the pending tasks and marks each one complete. instructions apply reports one of three states. It reports blocked when there is no task to work on, and ready when some tasks are open. It reports all done when no task is open, and in that state it tells the agent to review or verify. The developer's part is the second review of section 8.5: to read the evidence and not the ticks.

The validate command, run on a change that has not been archived, reads the delta and never the tasks, as section 8.2 says. The example's tasks run it as a check. openspec validate --strict fails on a warning, such as a requirement that says should where SHALL or MUST belongs. archive does not fail on it: it blocks on errors, and a warning passes it without being shown. The main specification then fails the strict check for the same warning. So a task that names "the command passing" is evidence about whichever form the task names.

The archive command reads the tasks to count them. It prints the count, and when some boxes are open it asks whether to continue. The default answer is no. A run with no one to answer is refused unless it is told to continue. The archive workflow reads the same count from list and asks the user to confirm before it continues. A change with no tasks.md, or with no checkbox in it, raises no question about the tasks. The archive command refuses a delta that it cannot merge, and it changes no file. When it succeeds, it moves the change into the archive under the date. The workflow stops before it moves the change if its merge fails. Sections 4.6 and 4.14 describe what that leaves in the main specification.

The tasks said how each decision is checked, and the workflows and the command described above use them. Chapters 9 to 12 describe what the tool does in each, who decides, and what to review. The frame of this chapter fits a file with parts, and it must be adapted for a workflow. Those chapters give each workflow a card, and a table of its stages or forms, in place of a file's parts.

The tasks are the checks of the design. An agent drafts them, a program counts them without being able to read them, and a person judges them by opening the evidence behind each box. The agent supplies the form of the template. The developer decides what counts as evidence and whether each task could have failed. The tool reads a number, so a tick is a claim. A claim whose evidence is the work itself, or cannot be found, is one that no one can check. A reading that someone who was not there can open is evidence, and so is a result that could have come out the other way. The review is made twice, before the work and when the boxes are ticked. The reason is that the tasks are the one artifact that changes after it is reviewed, and the ways to update them depend on whether a box is already ticked. The workflows and the command that follow count and move what the tasks record, and none of them verifies it. The reader should carry away two things. A list of ticked boxes shows that someone ticked. A task is done when its evidence can be opened and could have failed.

9. The Workflows and Who Does the Work

Chapters 4 to 8 followed one change from its first artifact to the archive, and they examined each of the four artifacts in detail. On the way, they met apply, validation and archive. These are not files, and the chapters gave each of them an outline. OpenSpec 2.1.1 defines twelve workflows, and this repository's profile installs seven of them. This chapter names those seven. It also names the one command that belongs to no workflow. Chapter 15 discusses the other five. This chapter asks four questions: what a workflow is, who does the work in it, which workflows a project has, and what the three chapters that follow are based on.

9.1 The workflows and the order a change meets them

The table lists the seven workflows and the validate command, in the order a change first meets them. It gives the entry point of each and a short description.

Workflow Entry point What it does
Explore the skill openspec-explore Think about a problem or idea with the agent before there is a change. It writes nothing unless the user confirms.
Propose the skill openspec-propose Create a change and all of its planning artifacts in one run.
Continue the skill openspec-continue-change Create the next missing artifact, one per run. Not in the core profile.
Update the skill openspec-update-change Revise the artifacts a change has, and make them agree.
Apply the skill openspec-apply-change Work through the tasks, and tick each box when its work is done.
Validate the command openspec validate Check the delta and the main specifications against the format rules. A command, not a workflow.
Sync the skill openspec-sync-specs Merge a change's delta into the main specifications without archiving the change.
Archive the skill openspec-archive-change and the command openspec archive Merge the delta unless told not to, count the tasks, and move the change into the archive.

The order of the table is a reading order, and the tool does not enforce any of it. Continue is another way of doing what propose does. Propose creates every planning artifact in one run, and continue creates one artifact in each run. Update and validate can be run again whenever the artifacts exist. Sync is optional, because archive can make the same merge. The skill openspec-apply-change, as OpenSpec 2.1.1 installs it, tells the agent that apply can be invoked at any time, as long as tasks exist. This includes the time before every artifact is done. OpenSpec's documentation calls its model "actions, not phases". Chapter 3 said the same of the artifacts, when it described their dependencies as enablers and not gates.

9.2 What a workflow consists of, and who acts in it

A workflow is delivered as a skill, and a skill is a text that the agent reads. The skill is a Markdown file in an .agents/skills/ folder, which is either the project's folder or the machine's, as chapter 3 describes. There is one folder for each workflow. The file begins with front matter, and the rest of it is instructions to the agent. In the seven skills this repository installs from OpenSpec 2.1.1, the front matter gives three things. It gives the skill's name, a description of what the skill is for and which words invoke it, and the one program the skill may run in a shell, openspec. The front matter also holds a licence, an author and a version of the skill's own. The skills of 2.0.0 also named the release that generated them, and the skills of 2.1.1 do not. The coding tool the book was checked with shows the model each skill's name and description each time it calls the model. It loads the body of a skill only when the model asks for it by name or the developer mentions it. The program does not run a skill. The agent reads the skill and does what it says.

The program contributes facts and checks. The skills installed by 2.1.1 tell the agent to ask a command, and not to assume. The skill openspec-propose tells the agent to run openspec context --json to find the project's root, and openspec new change to create a change. The skills tell the agent to run openspec status for the state of a change's artifacts. They tell it to run openspec instructions for the template and the instruction of an artifact. They tell it to run openspec instructions apply for the tasks and the count of tasks that are done. The skill openspec-archive-change tells the agent to run openspec list --json for a change's task counts. The skill openspec-sync-specs tells it to run openspec validate --specs after a merge. The skills also tell the agent not to assume names that the program knows. The skill openspec-continue-change says to use the schema's artifact sequence and not to assume artifact names. The skill openspec-apply-change says to use the files that the command returns and not to assume file names. The skill gives the order of the work, and the program gives the state that the work starts from.

The table says what each of the three parties does and what it leaves to the others.

Party Does Leaves to others
The agent Follows the skill: reads the files, calls the commands and writes the files. In the archive workflow, it can make the merge of a delta itself. The facts about the state of a change, which the program reports. Every decision, which the developer makes.
The program Reports the state and the counts, and checks the format. As the commands validate and archive, it checks a delta, can merge it, and moves a change into the archive. Reading the project and writing its files, which the agent does. Saying what is wanted, which the developer does.
The developer Decides what is wanted, confirms what a skill asks to have confirmed, and reviews the result. Writing the files, which the agent does. Checking the format, which the program does.

The same division holds in every workflow, but with a different weight. It is the pattern of chapter 3, and each workflow gives its three parties a different weight. In explore, the agent writes nothing until the developer confirms that it may. So the developer decides what is written, if anything is written. In propose, the agent writes every planning artifact. In validate, there is no skill, and the program does the work. In archive, the work can be done by the program or by the agent. The chapters that follow ask, for each workflow, who does what.

9.3 Which workflows are installed, and their names

No project has all twelve workflows unless its profile asks for them. OpenSpec installs the workflows that a setting called the profile asks for. The core profile installs six workflows:

  • propose: for when the developer can already say what is wanted.
  • explore: for when something has to be thought about carefully, before a change or during one.
  • apply: for when the plan is ready and the work starts, or when the work has to be resumed.
  • update: for when the plan has changed, or when an artifact was edited by hand and the others no longer agree with it.
  • sync: for when the main specifications should show a change before the change is archived.
  • archive: for when the work is finished and the change is to be closed.

Continue is not one of them, and this repository's profile adds it. The profile is a setting of the machine, not of one project. The command openspec update rewrites the installed skills so that they match the profile. A workflow whose skill is not installed cannot be called by its name.

Some of the names are easy to confuse:

  1. openspec update is a command that rewrites the installed skills. It is not the update workflow, which revises a change's artifacts.
  2. Archive is both a command and a workflow. The command is archive, and the workflow is archive. The table lists both as its entry points.
  3. Explore, apply and sync have no command of their own name. On 2.1.1, openspec apply, openspec sync and openspec explore each give an error, "unknown command".

For this reason, a workflow is written in plain text, and a command or a skill is written in code font.

9.4 What the next chapters do

What the next chapters say about a skill comes from reading it. What they say about a command comes from running it. Both the reading and the running were done on OpenSpec 2.1.1. A skill is a text, and one agent can follow the same text differently from another agent. The developer's review therefore covers that difference.

The next three chapters discuss the workflows in the order of the table, in three groups. The groups are the workflows that write the plan, the workflows that do the work and check it, and the workflows that make the project's record current. Each chapter begins with the table of section 9.1, with its own rows in bold. Each chapter asks the same four questions of every workflow:

  1. Who does the work?
  2. What does it read and write, and what can stop it?
  3. How does a reviewer judge what it did?
  4. What happens when its result is wrong?

Each workflow gets a card with the same five rows, so that the reader can compare one workflow with another.

Item What it says
Entry point The skill or the command that starts the workflow, and the words that call it.
Who acts Which of the agent, the program and the developer does each part of the work.
Writes The files that the workflow creates or changes, or the fact that it changes none.
What can stop it The check, the missing input or the question to the developer that stops it before it is done.
The developer's part What the developer decides, confirms or reviews, and what the workflow leaves to the developer.

The workflows that write the plan come first, because the reader already knows them by their results.

A workflow is a skill that the agent reads, together with the commands that the skill calls. The order of the table is not an order that the tool enforces. The question for the next chapters is who does the work in a workflow, because the answer differs. The agent writes in propose, the program checks in validate, and in archive the work can be done by the program or by the agent.

10. The Planning Workflows and What Each Leaves Behind

The previous chapter said who does the work in general. The agent follows a skill, the program reports facts and runs checks, and the developer decides and reviews. This chapter discusses the four workflows that write or revise the plan of a change: explore, propose, continue and update. For each one, it asks four questions. What does the developer do? What does the workflow write? How does a reviewer judge what it did? What happens when its result is wrong? The chapters on the four artifacts showed what the files contain. This chapter shows what creates them, and what the developer does while they are made.

The table lists the workflows and the validate command again. The four that this chapter discusses are in bold.

Workflow Entry point What it does
Explore the skill openspec-explore Think about a problem or idea with the agent before a change exists. It writes nothing unless the user confirms.
Propose the skill openspec-propose Create a change and all of its planning artifacts in one run.
Continue the skill openspec-continue-change Create the next missing artifact, one per run. Not in the core profile.
Update the skill openspec-update-change Revise the artifacts that a change has, and make them agree.
Apply the skill openspec-apply-change Work through the tasks, and tick each box when its work is done.
Validate the command openspec validate Check the delta and the main specifications against the format rules. A command, not a workflow.
Sync the skill openspec-sync-specs Merge the delta of a change into the main specifications without archiving the change.
Archive the skill openspec-archive-change and the command openspec archive Merge the delta unless told not to, count the tasks, and move the change into the archive.

10.1 Explore: thinking before a change exists

The skill openspec-explore, as OpenSpec 2.1.1 installs it, calls itself "a stance, not a workflow", and it has no stages. It tells the agent to think with the developer. The agent reads the project before it asks about anything it can find out itself. It asks one question at a time, and it never writes code. The skill allows writes only within a scope that the developer has confirmed. Before the first write, the agent names the files and asks for a yes or no in a separate message. An answer to a design question is never consent. There is one exception: the developer's own request to capture the exploration as a change. That request covers the change and the artifacts that the request names.

The card shows the five rows that the card of every workflow has.

Item Explore
Entry point The skill openspec-explore, called by its name or by the words "openspec explore" or "opsx explore".
Who acts The agent reads, asks and draws. The program answers read-only commands. The developer steers and confirms any write.
Writes Nothing, or the change and the artifacts that the developer confirmed.
What can stop it A project with no OpenSpec root, where the skill tells the agent to set nothing up. Or no yes before a write.
The developer's part To steer the thinking, to decide when it is enough, and to say yes or no to a write.

Explore has no stages to list. So the table says what explore may do, and what allows each action.

What explore may do What allows it What the tool checks
Read files and run read-only commands The skill, which needs no confirmation for a read list, list --specs and show change no file.
Scaffold a change The developer's request to capture the exploration, or a yes to an offer that named the change new change refuses a name that is already in use.
Write the artifacts that the request names The same request or yes, for those artifacts only Nothing at the write. Later, status counts a file as done if it exists.
Write anything else Nothing allows it Nothing.

The program supplies read-only facts: the active changes with their task counts, the capabilities, and the text of one specification. None of them changes a file. Nothing in the program keeps explore read-only. The stance belongs to the skill, and the program cannot see whether the agent kept it. In a directory with no root, the program answers no_openspec_root and creates nothing.

For the developer, explore is a conversation, and its only record is the conversation. Nothing is written until you say yes. So a decision you reached is not in the project until you ask for it to be captured. Before you give the yes, say which decisions to write and which change they belong to. That message is the scope of the yes. The skill tells the agent to ask again before it makes that scope wider. Do not answer a design question with a yes, because the skill treats such an answer as no consent. The tool gives no signal that the thinking is done. You decide when to stop. An exploration that never ends leaves nothing behind.

Explore leaves nothing unless something is captured. The skill ends in a proposal, in updated artifacts, or only in clarity. A decision that stays in the conversation is not in the archive. Chapter 3 said this, and this chapter does not repeat it.

10.2 Propose: the whole plan in one run

The skill openspec-propose, read on OpenSpec 2.1.1, creates a change and writes every artifact that the change needs in one run, in seven numbered stages. The agent asks the developer only about an ambiguity that would change the scope, the observable behaviour, the compatibility or the acceptance criteria. For a minor detail, it makes a reasonable assumption and records it in the artifacts. The request authorises planning only. The skill tells the agent to stop once the artifacts exist, and not to implement what the request asked to build. Sections 5.1, 6.1, 7.1 and 8.1 say who writes each artifact and what the developer's part in it is. This chapter does not repeat them.

The card shows the five rows for propose.

Item Propose
Entry point The skill openspec-propose, called by its name or by the words "openspec propose" or "opsx propose".
Who acts The agent writes. The program supplies the root, the build order, and the template and instruction of each artifact.
Writes The folder of the change and its .openspec.yaml, and every artifact in the required set. The exception is an artifact whose own instruction makes it conditional and that the agent reports as skipped.
What can stop it A project with no root, a name that is already in use, or a question that the agent asks about an ambiguity.
The developer's part The request, the answers to the questions, the assumptions in the drafts, and the review of each draft.

The table shows the seven stages of the skill, what the tool checks at each one, and the question that each one answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Understand the request and clarify material ambiguity Nothing. What is wanted, and what would change the scope if it were guessed wrong?
2. Load project context context --json returns the root, or no_openspec_root when there is none. Is there a project here, and what constraints does it set?
3. Determine the workflow schema schemas --json lists each schema and its artifacts. Which artifacts will this change have?
4. Create the change directory new change creates the folder and refuses a name that is already in use. Where there is no root, it creates one, so stage 2 comes first. Is there a place for the change?
5. Get the artifact build order status --json returns the status of each artifact, what it requires, and applyRequires. What can be written now, and what must exist before apply?
6. Create every artifact in the required set instructions <artifact> --json returns the template and the instruction. status runs again after each write. What goes into this file?
7. Show final status status reports each artifact and whether planning is complete. Is every artifact in the required set there?

For each artifact, instructions returns four things: the template, the instruction of the schema, the artifacts that it depends on, and the path of its file. When openspec/config.yaml has a context or rules, the command returns them too. The skill tells the agent that these are constraints and must not be copied into the file. The program does not check that the agent did not copy them.

Propose leaves a folder of files, and the program knows only whether each file exists. In a scratch project, a new change holds only .openspec.yaml, and the proposal is the only artifact that is ready. After the proposal, the specification and the design are ready. A specification is done as soon as one file matches its path, however many files the proposal named. A file of one character also counts as done. A change that declares skip_specs shows the specification as skipped from the start. Chapter 4 shows the four files of each of the two changes in the example in full.

For the developer, propose is one session of reading. The four drafts arrive together, so one review covers all of them. Read the proposal first, because the agent writes the other three from it. The minor assumptions are the part to check. The skill tells the agent to record them in the artifacts, and a reader who does not look for them will miss them. Then read the status. When an artifact is shown as skipped, the agent skipped it because of how it read the artifact's own instruction. In the default schema, the design is the artifact whose instruction makes it conditional. So decide whether you agree with the skip. Finally, check the working tree. A propose run should change only the folder of the new change. Commit the repository before the run, so that the diff shows what the run wrote.

10.3 Continue: one artifact at a time

The skill openspec-continue-change, on the same release, writes one artifact per run and then stops. It takes the first artifact whose status is ready and reads the files it depends on from disk. Then it writes the file and shows what the file unlocked. An earlier run may have stopped before it finished a specification. In that case the skill tells the agent to finish it first, and that counts as the one artifact of the run. If planning is already complete, the agent says so and writes nothing. When more than one change is active, the skill asks the developer which one to continue.

The card shows the five rows for continue.

Item Continue
Entry point The skill openspec-continue-change, called by its name or by the words "openspec continue" or "opsx continue". It is installed only in a profile that adds it.
Who acts The agent writes. The program reports the status and supplies the template and instruction.
Writes One artifact per run: the first that is ready, or the missing files of a specification that is partly written.
What can stop it Planning that is already complete, or no artifact that is ready.
The developer's part To choose the change when several are active, to read each draft before asking for the next, and to decide the pace.

The table shows the four stages of the skill, what the tool checks at each one, and the question that each one answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Select the change list --json returns the active changes, with the most recently modified first. Which change is meant?
2. Check current status status --json returns each artifact as done, ready, blocked or skipped, and whether planning is complete. What is next, and is anything left to write?
3. Act based on status instructions <artifact> --json returns the template and the instruction. What goes into this file?
4. After creating an artifact, show progress status runs again. It shows the artifact just written as done, and what it unlocked. What does the new file unlock?

The program decides what is next. The proposal is ready first. The specification and the design become ready after it, and the tasks wait for both. A skipped artifact never becomes ready. So the order of writing follows the schema, not the agent.

For the developer, continue gives a review point after each artifact, at the cost of one run for each. Read each draft before you ask for the next, because the agent writes the next artifact from it. There is one thing that status cannot show. A specification reads as done after one file. So after an interrupted run, count the files against the capabilities that the proposal lists. The rule is one spec.md for each capability, as chapter 6 said. A run that wrote one of three files leaves the specification looking finished. Ask for the next artifact only when you accept the draft you have.

10.4 Update: revising what exists

The skill openspec-update-change, on that release, revises the artifacts that exist and keeps them consistent. It drafts the requested edit in the conversation. It checks every other existing artifact against the edit, in either direction. It shows each proposed revision with its reason. It writes only after the developer confirms, one artifact at a time, and it never edits code. A request may change the intent of the change rather than its detail. In that case the skill tells the agent to recommend a new change under a new name.

The card shows the five rows for update.

Item Update
Entry point The skill openspec-update-change, called by its name or by the words "openspec update change" or "opsx update". It is not the command openspec update.
Who acts The agent drafts the revision and makes the artifacts agree. The developer confirms each write. The program reports which files exist.
Writes The artifact files that exist, and never code. After a confirmation, a missing file under a specification that already has one.
What can stop it A revision that the developer rejects, or a request that changes the intent.
The developer's part The revision, the confirmation of each write, and the decision on whether the intent has changed.

The table shows the six stages of the skill, what the tool checks at each one, and the question that each one answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Select the change list --json returns the active changes, with the most recently modified first. Which change is meant?
2. Get the change's artifacts status --json returns the status of each artifact and the files that exist. Which files can be revised?
3. Understand the request Nothing. Is this a specific revision, or a check that the artifacts agree?
4. Read and reconcile Nothing. The reading is the agent's. What else does the revision make wrong?
5. Confirm and apply, one artifact at a time Nothing. The confirmation is the developer's. instructions is called only for a substantial rewrite. Is each proposed revision accepted?
6. Point to what comes next Nothing. Which workflow follows?

Four of the six stages say "Nothing", and that is the point of the table. The decisions are the reading by the agent and the confirmation by the developer.

The program tracks files, not agreement. Take a scratch change whose tasks exist. An edit to its design changes no status, because every file still exists and every artifact is still done.

For the developer, update is where the reading happens, and no tool does it for you. Name the file, and say what must not change. Chapter 5 shows what happens when a request leaves that out. Read every proposed revision, including those to files you did not name. The skill checks the other artifacts in either direction, and a revision to one of them may be one you did not ask for. Reject any revision that goes beyond the request. Your request may change what the change is for. If it does, do not use update for it. Follow the recommendation of the skill and start a new change, so that the archive keeps the old one as it was.

10.5 What the planning workflows do not do

No planning workflow decides that the plan is right. The program reports that files exist. status reads no artifact for its content. validate reads the delta and the main specifications, and never the other three artifacts of an active change, as chapter 5 showed. The skills tell the agent to ask about an ambiguity. In explore and update, they also tell it to confirm a write. That is the agent asking, not the program checking. Chapter 8 said that the tool counts the boxes in the tasks and does nothing more. The review of the content is the developer's, with the checklists of the four artifact chapters.

Continue is not in the core profile, and the choice between propose and continue is a choice about review points. A project on the core profile has propose and update, and no continue. Propose writes every artifact in one run, so the first review covers all of them together. Continue gives a review between artifacts, at the cost of one run for each. The profile of this repository adds continue. The repository also has a rule that the owner approves the outline of a chapter before any prose is written. That rule is a review point of the kind that one artifact per run gives. Neither way is better in itself. The difference is where the developer reads.

10.6 Reviewing what a planning workflow did

This review asks whether the workflow did what its skill told the agent to do. It does not ask whether the file is right; the checklists of the four artifact chapters ask that. The review has four passes. Authority asks whether each write was requested or confirmed. Coverage asks whether every artifact that the plan needs exists, and whether each was written from the one it depends on. Record asks whether every decision made in the conversation reached a file. Order asks whether each artifact was written after the ones it depends on, and whether the context and rules of the project were kept out of it. Record and Authority matter most, because the program sees neither. It sees which files exist and which artifacts are blocked. It does not see who asked for a write, or a decision that stayed in the conversation.

The table is one checklist, in the order in which a change is made.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which request the run answers, and nothing in the files answers an assumption made instead The run serves an assumption that the developer did not make, and every artifact after it follows the assumption
Explore wrote nothing without a yes Every file that explore wrote is one that the developer asked for or confirmed A file was written because of an answer to a design question, or beyond what the confirmation named
Propose wrote the required set and implemented nothing Each artifact of the required set exists or was reported as skipped, and nothing outside the folder of the change was edited An artifact is missing although no skip was reported, or code was edited because the request asked for something to be built
Continue wrote one artifact One new artifact exists since the last run, and it is the first that was ready Two artifacts were written in one run, or one was written before the ones it depends on
Update changed only what was confirmed, and no code Each changed file is one whose revision the developer confirmed, and no code changed A file changed that was not shown, or a rejected revision was written anyway
No context or rules text was copied into an artifact The artifacts say what the change is, and do not repeat the constraints of the project A constraint from the configuration was copied into a file as if it were content
A decision made in the conversation is in a file Each decision that the developer remembers making is written in the artifact that owns it The decision was settled in the conversation and no file records it, so the archive will not hold it
Downstream The artifacts are ready for the reviews of the four artifact chapters Every file exists, and the plan has still not been reviewed

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. When the status of a change shows every artifact as done, the change has its files. It does not necessarily have a reviewed plan.

The developer can follow one routine for all four workflows:

  1. Commit the repository before a run, so that the changes of the run show as one diff.
  2. Say in one sentence what the run is for, and what must not change.
  3. After the run, read status and the list of changed files. A changed file outside the folder of the change, or any change under code, is a reason to stop and ask.
  4. Read the drafts in the order of their dependencies: the proposal first, then the artifacts written from it.
  5. Confirm, or revise. Revise by hand when the fix is one phrase. Ask for a revision when several files have to agree.
  6. Commit again once you have read the drafts, so that the next run starts from a reviewed state.

10.7 Changing the result

When the review finds that a planning workflow went wrong, the developer makes two decisions: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first decision depends on what already exists.

What exists What the revision covers
Only an exploration, with nothing written Nothing to revise. The conversation continues, or propose writes the plan. This is a new run, not an edit.
Drafts written and not yet reviewed An edit to the draft at its own part, by the paths of the chapter on that artifact.
Drafts reviewed, and later artifacts written from them An update that reconciles forwards: the artifacts written from the changed one are revised too, by the paths of the chapters on those artifacts.
Tasks ticked, and apply begun The update, and then a check of what apply has done. The skill says that the code may no longer match the revised plan.
The change archived Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example shows the last row and none of the others. Section 4.8 of chapter 4 says that the correction of the first change was made in a second change, because the first had been archived. The archive holds no revision of a draft. So the other rows are described and not shown.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the artifact by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. The two ways differ in cost and in how they go wrong.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when The edit is one phrase that the developer can write without help Several artifacts have to agree, or the right text has to be worked out from the others
What it costs The developer's reading of every artifact that depends on the one changed A confirmation for each write, and a request that says what must not change
How it goes wrong A dependent artifact is left as it was, so the files disagree The agent misses a file when it makes the artifacts agree, or someone gives a confirmation without reading what it confirms
What to check afterwards The diff, and each artifact written from the one that changed Each confirmed diff, and the artifacts that were not named

Suppose the developer changes one decision in the design of a vending machine change: the machine now works out the change before it releases the product. The developer edits nothing else. By hand, the tasks are left as they were. status still shows every artifact done, because every file exists. The tasks still check the order that the design had before. The diff of the design shows the new decision. It does not show the task that checks the old one.

Suppose, instead, that the developer asks the update workflow to make the tasks agree with the changed decision. The skill tells the agent to draft the edit, to check the other artifacts against it, and to show each proposed revision. The developer decides which revisions to confirm. The tasks that checked the old decision are reopened or rewritten. A ticked box is the part that the diff shows least.

The developer checks both means in the same way: by the diff, and by reading what depends on the file that changed. The status shows that files exist, and the diff shows words. Neither shows that the artifacts agree. Read a revision as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

10.8 What the planning workflows pass on

The planning workflows pass the plan to apply. The artifacts are the input of apply, and apply requires the tasks. Apply reads the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks. A plan that the developer has not reviewed is passed on as it is, because nothing in the program stops it.

The next chapter discusses the workflow that does the work and the command that checks the plan: apply and validate.

The planning workflows write a plan, and the program can see only which of its files exist. So the developer must judge the plan. A change whose artifacts all exist is not a change whose plan is right.

11. Apply and Validate, and What a Tick and a Pass Show

The previous chapter discussed the four workflows that write or revise a plan. It ended when the plan was passed to the workflow that carries it out. This chapter discusses the next two entries of the table. Apply is the workflow that does the work and ticks the boxes. validate is the command that checks the form of the delta and the main specifications. They share a chapter because each leaves a result that a reader can take for more than it is: a count of ticks, and a pass. For each, the chapter asks four questions. What does the developer do? What does it read and write, and what can stop it? How does a reviewer judge what it did? What happens when its result is wrong? The examples are the tasks files of the vending machine's two changes, which hold ticks and no code. A scratch project, in which the commands were run, supplies the rest.

The table lists the workflows and the validate command again. Apply and validate are in bold.

Workflow Entry point What it does
Explore the skill openspec-explore Think about a problem or idea with the agent before there is a change. It writes nothing unless the user confirms.
Propose the skill openspec-propose Create a change and all of its planning artifacts in one run.
Continue the skill openspec-continue-change Create the next missing artifact, one per run. Not in the core profile.
Update the skill openspec-update-change Revise the artifacts a change has and make them agree.
Apply the skill openspec-apply-change Work through the tasks and tick each box when its work is done.
Validate the command openspec validate Check the delta and the main specifications against the format rules. A command, not a workflow.
Sync the skill openspec-sync-specs Merge a change's delta into the main specifications without archiving it.
Archive the skill openspec-archive-change and the command openspec archive Merge the delta unless told not to, count the tasks, and move the change into the archive.

11.1 Apply: working through the tasks

The skill openspec-apply-change, as OpenSpec 2.1.1 installs it, tells the agent to carry out the plan one task at a time. The agent selects the change and asks the program for the apply instructions. It reads the context files that the instructions list. Then it works on each pending task in turn. For each task, it shows which task it is on, keeps the change minimal, ticks the box, and asks for the instructions again. It stops and asks in five cases: when a task is unclear, when the work shows a design issue, when a task needs work that the plan does not describe, when an error occurs, and when the developer interrupts. Section 8.1 says who ticks the boxes and what that means for the evidence. This chapter does not repeat it.

The card shows the five rows for apply.

Item Apply
Entry point The skill openspec-apply-change, called by its name or by the words "openspec apply", "opsx apply" or "openspec implement". The command openspec instructions apply serves it.
Who acts The agent works and ticks the boxes. The program reports the state, the progress and the line of each task. The developer decides at each pause.
Writes The work that the tasks name, and a tick in the box of each finished task.
What can stop it A blocked state, a pause that the skill names, an error, or an interruption.
The developer's part To decide at each pause, and to judge each tick against its evidence.

The table shows the seven stages of the skill, what the tool checks at each, and the question each answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Select the change list --json returns the active changes. Which change is meant?
2. Check the status to understand the schema status --json returns the schema's name and which artifact holds the tasks. Which schema is in use, and which file holds the tasks?
3. Get the apply instructions instructions apply --json returns the state, the context files, the progress, and each task with its source path and line. Can the work begin, and what is the list?
4. Read the context files Nothing. What does the plan say?
5. Show the current progress The count in the same output: the total, the tasks complete and the tasks remaining. How much is done?
6. Implement the tasks, in a loop After each tick, instructions apply reports the count again. It does not read the work. Did the tick register?
7. Show the status on completion or pause The same count, and the state all done when no box is open. Where does the work stand, and why did it stop?

The program reports a state and a count, and it checks only that a tick registers. At stage 6, the skill tells the agent to confirm that the box at the returned line still matches the task. The agent then ticks it and asks for the instructions again, to confirm that the task is done and the progress has changed. In a scratch project, ticking one of two boxes changed the count from one complete to two. It changed the state from ready to all done. Each returned line was the line of its box. A paragraph added above the tasks moved both returned lines by two. For this reason, the skill tells the agent to use the line that the program returns, and not a line it remembers. The check is that the box reads as done, not that the work is done. The instructions also return the project's context when the configuration has one. The skill says that this and the optional operationGuidance input are not evidence of task completion. Section 8.7 describes the three states, and this chapter does not repeat them.

The skill gives the agent two kinds of rule, and the program checks neither. The first is the rule for a tick. Its guardrail in the skill of 2.1.1 reads "Only mark a task - [x] when its specified behavior is fully implemented, not when it is partially done or deferred". A box is ticked when the behaviour is fully done, and not before. The second kind is the rules for pausing. A task may need work beyond what the specification and the tasks describe. Or the agent may be tempted to drop, narrow or defer specified behaviour, or to accept an exception to it, to make the work fit. In both cases, the skill tells the agent to report the added scope and ask, and not to include it silently. When the work meets a design issue, the skill tells the agent to suggest updating the artifacts. Each of these is an instruction to the agent. The program has no way to see whether the agent followed it.

The schema defines apply, and apply is not a gate. The schema's apply block says three things: what apply requires, which file it tracks, and what instruction it gives. The spec-driven schema requires the tasks and tracks tasks.md. Its instruction is two sentences. They tell the agent to work on the pending tasks in turn, to mark each one complete, and to pause on a blocker or a need for clarification. This project's book-change schema is a fork, as chapter 3 described. Its apply instruction is its own, so a fork changes what apply tells the agent. The skill says that apply can be invoked at any time, as long as tasks exist. This includes the time before every artifact is done. The skill also says that apply can be mixed with updates. In a scratch change that held only a tasks file, instructions apply reported the state ready. It listed the proposal, the specification and the design as missing prerequisites. It warned that the change had no delta specification. The program asks for the tasks, not for a complete plan.

The example shows the ticks and no code. Both archived tasks files of the vending machine have every box ticked. The first change's file has three tasks, and the second change's file has five. The second change was made after the first change had been archived, as section 4.8 says. The example has no code, so the archive holds only the ticks and the evidence that each task names. Sections 4.5 and 4.12 show the two files in full, and chapter 8 examines them in detail.

For the developer, apply is where a plan becomes work. The review of what it did is the second review of section 8.5. Commit the repository before the run, so that the diff shows what the run changed. Name the change that the run is for. When the skill pauses, the pause is a question for you. The answers that matter are about scope. A task that needs more than the plan describes is a decision for the developer. A design issue is a reason to revise the artifacts before the work continues. After the run, read the diff beside the ticks, task by task. A box that is ticked with no change in the diff is a question to ask. So is a change that no task names. The state all done means that no box is open. The review that the skill asks for at that point is yours.

11.2 Validate: checking the form of the delta

validate is a command, and OpenSpec 2.1.1 has no skill for it. The program does the work, and something else runs it. The developer runs it, or a task names it. The skill openspec-sync-specs tells the agent to run openspec validate --specs after a merge. An agent runs it only when a task or a skill says so. The developer needs to know which form was run, because the forms check different things.

The card shows the five rows for validate.

Item Validate
Entry point The command openspec validate, with a name or an option. It has no skill.
Who acts The program checks. A developer, a task or another workflow runs it.
Writes Nothing. In a scratch project, runs of the plain, strict, bulk and archived forms left every file unchanged.
What can stop it An error, which ends the run with a failure. With --strict, a warning does too. A run with no name, no option and no one to ask prints what to try and fails.
The developer's part To read the result, and to know what the form that was run covers.

A command has no stages. So the table shows its forms, what each checks, and the question each answers.

Form What it checks The question it answers
openspec validate <change> The change's delta against the form rules of chapter 6, and the main specification that a MODIFIED requirement names. A MODIFIED requirement that the main specification lacks passes, with a note that the archive would refuse the delta. Is this delta well formed?
openspec validate <specification> One main specification against the same rules. Is this specification well formed?
--changes Every active change, with one result for each. Archived changes are not read. Are all the deltas well formed?
--specs Every main specification. Are all the specifications well formed?
--all The active changes and the main specifications. Is everything well formed?
--strict Added to any form: a warning fails as an error does. Is it free of warnings too?
--json Added to any form: the same checks, with the result as data. Each item has its type, whether it is valid, and its issues. Each issue has a level, a path and a message, and the totals follow. Can a script read the result?
--archived The archived changes only: that the tasks.md of each has no open box. It reads no delta. Was every task of each archived change ticked?

The options --type, --report, --concurrency, --no-interactive and --store are in the command's help. This chapter does not use them.

validate reads the delta and the main specifications. For an active change, the forms above do not open proposal.md, design.md or tasks.md. In a scratch change with no proposal, no design and an empty tasks.md, the command reported the change valid. The one form that opens a tasks.md is --archived, and it opens only archived ones. Chapters 4, 6 and 8 say what each file leaves to a person. Section 6.2 says what the delta is checked for. So chapter 11 adds nothing to them. An error and a warning differ in what they stop. An error fails the run in every form. A warning passes the plain form and fails the strict one. A note changes neither, such as the note for a MODIFIED requirement that is absent.

A pass is about the form of the delta, and the example's first change shows what that leaves out. Both tasks files of the example end with a task that names openspec validate --strict passing. That is evidence about the delta and about nothing else. The first change passed validation and every task. Still, a case that no one had written defeated its design. Section 4.5 says so, and section 4.7 goes through the case.

validate can be a gate. The command's help describes --archived as a check for pre-commit linting. --json lets a script read the result as data and not as text. If a form is run before archiving, that form becomes a precondition of the archive. This project's book-change schema asks every change for a review task that runs openspec validate --all --strict. That is a use of the command, and not advice about your use of it. The gate checks form. --all reads the active changes and the main specifications, so it opens no archived tasks.md. That check is the form --archived. Run against the example, --archived passed both archived changes, because both files have all their boxes ticked.

For the developer, validate is a quick check with a narrow answer. Know which form you ran. Read the whole result, not only the last line. An error, a warning and a note mean different things, and the note is the only place where the command says that the archive would refuse a delta. Run it again after any change to a delta, because a pass before the change says nothing about the delta after it. When the result is a pass, say what it covers: the delta is well formed. It says nothing about the design, the tasks or the work.

11.3 What apply and validate do not check

Neither apply nor validate checks that the work is right. Apply's result is ticks. The work is the agent's, and the program counts and reports. validate is structural, and it depends on neither the design nor the tasks of the change. No workflow in this chapter runs a project's tests or turns a scenario into a test. A specification defines the expected behaviour, and tests and verification still have to check it, as chapter 2 says. A pass of validation is no verdict on the requirements, as chapter 3 says. A project that has code has its own tests, and the example has none.

11.4 Reviewing what apply and validate did

This review asks whether apply and validate did what their rules say. It does not ask whether the work is right. That question is for the project's own tests and for the second review of section 8.5. The review has four passes. Evidence asks whether each tick is backed by evidence that could have failed, as section 8.5 describes. Scope asks whether anything was done that the plan does not name, or dropped that the plan does name. Form asks whether validate was run, in which form, and on what. Return asks whether a design issue found in the work went back to the artifacts. Evidence and Scope matter most. The program counts the ticks and checks the form, and it sees neither evidence nor scope.

The table is one checklist, in the order in which the work is done.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which change and which tasks the run answers, and the work follows the plan, not an assumption The run serves the tasks of another change, or an assumption that the developer did not make
Apply read the context files and worked task by task Each task has its own change in the diff, in the order of the list One change covers several tasks, or boxes were ticked together after the work
Each tick matches its task and its evidence Each tick has its evidence where its task says to look, and the evidence could have failed A ticked box lacks the evidence that its task names, or the evidence is the work itself
No behaviour was narrowed or deferred Each behaviour that the delta names is in the work, and any added scope was put to the developer A behaviour was dropped, narrowed or deferred under a ticked box, or work that no task names was done
A pause was resolved by the developer Each question that the work raised has an answer from the developer, in the conversation or in an artifact A question was settled without the developer, or the answer stayed in the conversation and no file holds it
A design issue went back to the artifacts The artifacts say what the work now does, and the boxes that depended on the old plan were reopened The work avoided the issue, and the design still states the old decision
validate was run in the form the project uses The form is the one that the project names, run on the files as they are now A form that does not read the changed files was run, or the result is older than the last change to the delta
The result is read as being about form The pass is reported as covering the delta and the main specifications A pass is read as showing that the design, the tasks or the work are right
Downstream Every box is ticked with its evidence and the delta is valid, so the change is ready for archive The count is complete and the delta is valid, and neither says that the work is right

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A reader can take a complete count and a pass as the whole of the review, and neither is. A result is accepted when a person has read what is behind it.

For both apply and validate, the developer can follow one routine:

  1. Commit the repository before apply runs, so that the run's changes show as one diff.
  2. Name the change that the run is for, and read its tasks first, so that you know what evidence each tick should have.
