  3. Answer each pause as a decision. If the work shows a design issue, revise the artifacts before apply continues.
  4. After the run, read the diff beside the ticks, task by task, and open the evidence that each task names.
  5. Run validate in the form the project uses, and read the whole result, including any note.
  6. Commit once you have read the result, so that the next run starts from a state that has been reviewed.

11.5 Changing the result

When the review finds that apply or validate went wrong, two decisions follow. The first is what the revision covers. The second is who makes it. The first depends on how far the work has gone.

What exists What the revision covers
No box ticked An edit of the plan, by the paths of the chapter on that artifact, and then apply from the start.
Some boxes ticked The same edit, and the ticked tasks that depend on it are reopened, as section 8.6 says.
Every box ticked The same, and apply is run again. In a scratch change, one reopened box changed the state from all done back to ready.
A failing validation A fix in the delta, by the path of chapter 6, and validation run again.
The change archived Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example shows the last row and none of the others. Section 4.8 says that the first change was corrected in a second change, because the first had been archived. Section 8.6 says that the first change's list was left unchanged, with all its boxes still ticked. The other rows are absent from the archive. Section 8.6 gives the reason for its own middle row. A failing validation writes no file for an archive to keep.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the files by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. The two means differ in cost and in how they fail.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when One box or one word is wrong and the developer knows the replacement A task has to be done again, or several tasks and the work have to change together
What it costs The developer's reading of each task that depends on the one changed A run, and a request that says which tasks to redo and what must not change
How it goes wrong A dependent box is left ticked on evidence that no longer fits The box is ticked again over the same evidence, or the run does more than the request named
What to check afterwards The diff, and each box that depends on the one changed Each reopened box against its new evidence, and the files outside the tasks that the run named

Suppose the developer revises the design of a vending machine change, so that the machine checks the coins it holds before it accepts the payment. The developer then finds that the ticked task that traces a scenario through the design no longer fits. By hand, the developer reopens the box and rewrites the task so that it names the revised design. The diff shows the box and the words. It does not show that a later box was ticked based on the trace that has changed.

Suppose apply stops over a design issue, as the skill's rule for a pause allows. The developer revises the plan with the update workflow, as the previous chapter described, and then asks for apply again. The boxes that were ticked against the old plan are the ones to reopen before the work continues.

Both means are checked in the same way: by the diff, and by running validate again for the delta. For an active change, the program reads neither the tasks nor the design, so a pass is about the delta's form alone. A revision to a tick is read as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

11.6 What apply and validate pass on

Apply and validate pass two things to archive: a ticked list and a delta that is well formed. Neither is a statement about the work or about the evidence behind it. A reviewer who takes the two results as the whole review passes archive a change that has not been checked.

The next chapter discusses the workflows that merge the delta and close the change: sync and archive.

Apply is an agent that works to a skill's rules while the program counts the boxes. validate is the program checking the form of the delta and the main specifications. Neither reads whether the work is right. A change whose boxes are all ticked and whose delta passes has a count and a pass. The evidence and the scope behind them are for the developer to review.

12. Sync and Archive, and the Record They Leave

The previous chapter ended with a ticked list and a well-formed delta, passed to the workflows that make the record current. This chapter discusses the last two entries of the table. Sync is the workflow that merges a delta into the main specifications and leaves the change open. Archive merges unless it is told not to, and it moves the change into the archive. The two share a chapter for two reasons. They leave the same thing: the main specifications that every later change is checked against. And archive has two answers to the first question, who does the work. For each of them the chapter asks four questions. What does the developer do? What does it read and write, and what can stop it? How does a reviewer judge what it did? What happens when its result is wrong? The examples are the vending machine's main specification and archived changes, and a scratch project in which the commands were run.

The table lists the workflows and the validate command again. Sync and archive are in bold.

Workflow Entry point What it does
Explore the skill openspec-explore Think about a problem or idea with the agent before there is a change. It writes nothing unless the user confirms.
Propose the skill openspec-propose Create a change and all of its planning artifacts in one run.
Continue the skill openspec-continue-change Create the next missing artifact, one per run. Not in the core profile.
Update the skill openspec-update-change Revise the artifacts a change has and make them agree.
Apply the skill openspec-apply-change Work through the tasks and tick each box when its work is done.
Validate the command openspec validate Check the delta and the main specifications against the format rules. A command, not a workflow.
Sync the skill openspec-sync-specs Merge a change's delta into the main specifications without archiving it.
Archive the skill openspec-archive-change and the command openspec archive Merge the delta unless told not to, count the tasks, and move the change into the archive.

12.1 Sync: merging without closing the change

The skill openspec-sync-specs, as OpenSpec 2.1.1 installs it, tells the agent to merge each delta of a change into its main specification. It also tells the agent to keep everything the delta does not mention. The agent selects the change. It asks the program where the main specifications are and which deltas exist. It reads each delta and its main specification. It applies the four operations as a merge and not as a copy. It then validates the main specifications and shows what changed. The skill calls the operation agent-driven, so that a delta can add one scenario to a requirement without a copy of the whole requirement. For a modified requirement, the closing principle of the same skill says the opposite of that last point. A MODIFIED block carries the whole requirement, and validate and archive both reject a block that drops a scenario the main specification still has. The skill stops in three cases: when the change has no delta, when the lookup of the rules fails, and when a capability is blocked. Chapter 6 says what the operations of a delta are, and this chapter does not repeat it.

The card shows the five rows for sync.

Item Sync
Entry point The skill openspec-sync-specs, called by its name or by the words "openspec sync" or "opsx sync". No command has that name.
Who acts The agent merges. The program supplies the paths and the rules, and validates the main specifications afterwards. The developer decides to sync and reads the result.
Writes The main specifications that the delta names, and nothing else. The change folder is not touched.
What can stop it A change with no delta, a failed lookup of the rules, a capability that is blocked, or a failed validation.
The developer's part To decide whether to merge before the change is archived, and to read the merge.

The table shows the six stages of the skill, what the tool checks at each, and the question each answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Select the change list --json returns the active changes, and the skill offers those that have a delta. Which change is meant?
2. Resolve the change context status --json returns the root under which the main specifications are. Where are the main specifications?
3. Find the delta specifications status --json returns the delta paths that exist. The skill uses no other source. Which deltas does the change hold?
4. Apply each delta instructions specs --json returns the rules that the project configured for specifications, once, before the first write. Nothing reads the merge. Does the main specification say what the delta says?
5. Validate the main specifications validate --specs checks the form of every main specification. Is the result well formed?
6. Show the summary Nothing. What changed, and what is left to write?

The program supplies two things and checks one. At stage 4 it supplies the rules, and nothing reads the merge itself. The check is at stage 5. It is about the form of the main specifications, not about whether the merge says what the delta says. In a scratch project, status reported the root and the one delta path that existed. instructions specs returned a rules list only after the project's configuration named a rule. openspec sync was an unknown command, so the skill is the only definition of sync.

The skill gives a rule for each operation. The rules say what the main specification should hold afterwards and when the merge stops. The table shows them.

Operation What sync does When it stops
ADDED Adds the requirement. If one of that name exists, it updates it to match. Not by itself.
MODIFIED Finds the requirement and applies the change: a new scenario, a changed scenario or a changed description. It keeps the text the delta does not mention. It expects the block to carry every scenario the main specification has: validate and archive reject a block that drops one. In a scratch project on 2.1.1, the first rejected it at validation, and the second by stopping with no file changed. When the capability has no main specification. For a capability that has one, the skill says to find the requirement and says nothing about one that is missing; the command refuses that delta.
REMOVED Removes the whole requirement block. It removes the capability's spec.md only when six conditions hold, among them that no requirement is left, that the rest of the file is well formed, and that the change's .openspec.yaml declares retire_capabilities: true. When the capability has no main specification: there it skips the operation and warns. When removing would leave no requirement and a condition fails, it changes nothing for that capability and names the condition. It never leaves an empty ## Requirements section.
RENAMED Finds the requirement under its old name and gives it the new one. When the capability has no main specification.
Purpose For a new capability, copies the delta's Purpose word for word, and writes a placeholder only when the delta has none. For an existing one, leaves the main specification's Purpose unchanged. Never.

For a capability with no main specification, only ADDED requirements can create it. MODIFIED and RENAMED have no requirement to act on there. For them, the skill tells the agent to stop for that capability and never to invent the missing requirement. REMOVED has nothing to remove, and the skill tells the agent to skip it and warn. The merge creates the file with a title, the delta's Purpose and the requirements. Section 4.6 shows the first lines of the file as the first change left them. The skill says that the merge it describes matches what openspec archive does for a new capability and for the Purpose. It claims no more than that.

Sync leaves the change open and the main specification ahead of it. After a sync, the main specification holds the new requirement. The change folder is where it was, and its tasks are as they were. That is why sync is optional: archive can make the same merge, and its workflow offers to. It also means that the next person can read the main specification between the sync and the archive, before the change is done.

For the developer, sync is a decision to make the record current before the change is closed. Commit the repository before the run, so that the merge shows as a diff of the main specifications and of nothing else. Name the change. When it has several deltas, say which of them are to be merged. Write a modified requirement whole, as chapter 6 teaches. Do not rely on the merge to keep a scenario that the block left out, because the program rejects such a block. After the run, read the diff of the main specifications beside the delta, operation by operation. Read a modified requirement whole in the main specification, because a diff shows only the words that moved. Read the summary for a Purpose that was left as a placeholder, because no later step asks anyone to write it.

12.2 Archive: merging and moving the change

Two parties can archive a change, and they do not do the same thing. The command openspec archive does everything in the program. The skill openspec-archive-change tells the agent to do several things in turn. The agent reads the status and the task count, and asks the user to confirm what is open. It compares each delta with its main specification and offers a sync. It runs the sync workflow inline. It checks the result against the delta, and it moves the folder. So the question of who does the work has two answers. The first is the program. The second is the agent, with the program's counts. The rest of this section says which of the two each sentence is about. The developer decides which to use, answers what is asked, and reads the main specification afterwards.

The card shows the five rows for archive, with an answer for each path where they differ.

Item Archive
Entry point The command openspec archive, and the skill openspec-archive-change.
Who acts The command: the program. The workflow: the agent, with the program's counts and the validation inside the sync. The developer chooses the path and answers what it asks.
Writes The main specifications that the delta names, and the change folder, which is moved into archive under its date.
What can stop it A delta that fails validation or cannot be merged, a question that is answered no or not answered, a mismatch after a merge, a failed lookup, or an archive of the same name.
The developer's part To choose the path, to answer what it asks, and to read the record.

The table shows the six stages of the archive workflow, what the tool checks at each, and the question each answers.

Stage What the tool checks The question it answers
1. Select the change, and read the archive inputs list --json returns the active changes. instructions archive --json is advisory: in the scratch project it returned the change's name and the root. It carries project context or guidance only when the project adds them. Which change is meant, and what does the project add?
2. Check the artifact status status --json lists each artifact as done, skipped or neither. Is the plan complete? The skill asks the user to confirm if it is not.
3. Check the task count list --json returns the total and the completed count; only x and X count as complete. Is the work ticked? The skill asks the user to confirm if it is not.
4. Assess the delta, and sync if chosen Nothing: the agent checks that the archive target is free before any main specification is written. instructions specs --json returns the rules once before a sync, and stage 5 of the sync runs validate --specs. The comparison of the delta with the main specification is the agent's. Does the main specification need the merge, and does it hold it afterwards?
5. Perform the archive Nothing: the skill checks the target once more, moves the folder with mv, and fails if the target exists. Is the change in the archive under its date?
6. Display the summary Nothing. What happened, and with what warnings?

The sync inside stage 4 is the sync workflow of the previous section, not a command. The skill tells the agent to run it inline and to wait. The reason is that a move of the folder while a sync is still reading it would leave the change archived and the main specifications never updated. After the sync, the skill tells the agent to check the structure of each main specification. It also tells the agent to confirm that no delta heading remains, and to compare every capability with its delta again. If anything differs, the agent stops, and nothing has moved.

The two paths differ in who merges, in what is checked and in what stops them. The table shows them side by side. The column for the command is what was run in a scratch project on OpenSpec 2.1.1. The column for the workflow is what the skill tells the agent to do; no agent was run.

What The archive command The archive workflow
Who merges The program. The agent, following the sync workflow inline. Where that skill is not installed, the agent merges itself under the same safeguards and then runs validate --specs.
Whether the change is passed through validate Yes, first, when there is a delta. An error stops it before the task line is printed. The skill names no validate run on the change. It runs validate --specs on the main specifications, inside the sync.
Where the task count comes from The command reads the tasks file and prints a line, for example "Task status: 1/2 tasks". list --json, with the total and the completed count. The skill stops if the lookup fails or the counts are invalid.
Whether artifact completion is checked No. In the scratch project, a change with one of four artifacts complete was archived on --yes. The command printed no warning about the missing artifacts. Yes. The skill reads status --json and asks the user to confirm if an artifact is neither done nor skipped.
What asks the user, and the default "Continue?" for open tasks, with the default no, and "Proceed with spec updates?", with the default yes. With no one to answer, it fails and names --yes. The same two matters, as confirmations. Also a choice of "Sync now", "Archive without syncing" or "Cancel", or of "Archive now", "Sync anyway" or "Cancel" when the delta is already merged. The skill asks again on any other answer.
A delta that cannot be merged It refuses, prints "Aborted. No files were changed.", and the change stays. A capability that cannot be merged is marked blocked, and only "Archive without syncing" and "Cancel" are offered. If the sync reports a stop, the archive stops with nothing moved.
What is checked after the merge Before it writes, the command validates the rebuilt main specification, and writes nothing if that fails. After it writes, the skill checks the structure, confirms no delta heading remains, and compares each capability with its delta again. The sync runs validate --specs.
How the folder is moved and named In the program, under the date. It fails with "Archive ... already exists" when the name is taken, and the change stays. With mv, after it makes the archive directory, under the date, never with a second date added. It checks that the target is free before it writes any main specification and again before the move. If the target is not free, it stops with the change in place.
The options that skip a check --yes, --skip-specs and --no-validate. The answer "Archive without syncing", and the answers to each confirmation.

Both paths can skip a check, and the developer decides which one. The command's help describes --yes as skipping the confirmation prompts and --skip-specs as skipping the spec update operations. It describes --no-validate as skipping validation, calls that not recommended, and says it requires confirmation. In the scratch project, --skip-specs moved a change whose delta was never merged. --no-validate merged a requirement that had no scenario. The main specification then failed validate --specs. The next archive of a change that touched it was refused until the requirement was removed. The program reports what it was told to skip, and does not say whether the skip was right.

For the developer, archive is where the change stops being work and the record changes, and the review is of what the merge left. Choose the path before the run, and know what each path checks. The command validates the delta and the rebuilt specification before it writes anything. The workflow compares the result with the delta after it writes. Answer each question as a decision. Read the question that defaults to yes, the merge, as carefully as the one that defaults to no, the open tasks. Commit the repository before the run, so that the merge and the move show as one diff.

The example shows what an archive leaves, and nothing of the path. After the first change, the main specification purchase holds the first change's requirements and nothing about the change that wrote them. The folder with the proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks is in the archive under its date. Section 4.6 shows both. After the second change, the modified requirement is replaced and the file has no new section, as section 4.14 says. The archived folders hold the artifacts and a metadata file. That file records the schema and the date the change was created. None of the files says which path made the record, or whether a check was skipped.

An archive is a record, and nothing in it is edited. A change that has been moved into the archive is not changed again. An archived design that was wrong stays as it was, and a new change corrects it. Chapter 5 says so for the proposal, and section 4.8 shows it: the first change's requirement was found incomplete, and the correction was a second change. The only form of validate that reads the archive is --archived. It checks that each archived tasks.md has no open box.

12.3 What sync and archive do not check

Neither path checks whether the record is right. The program checks the form of the delta and of the main specifications. The agent compares its own merge with the delta. Neither path asks whether the requirement that reached the main specification is the right one. Section 4.14 says why that matters: every later change relies on what the record holds, so an error in it is carried forward. Also, the two paths need not give the same result. Sync has no command, so the sync workflow has the skill's rules and nothing that checks them. The skill's statement that it matches the command is the skill's own claim.

12.4 Reviewing the record

This review asks whether sync and archive did what their rules say. It does not ask whether the requirement is right; that is for the review of the delta in chapter 6. The review has four passes. Merge asks whether the main specification says what the delta says and no more, with everything else kept. Form asks four things: that no delta heading remains, that the Purpose is not a placeholder, that the file has the format of a main specification, and that validate passes. Folder asks whether the change is in the archive under its date with all its artifacts. Path asks which path was used and which checks were skipped. Merge and Path matter most. The reason is that the program checks the form and not the content, and a skipped check leaves no record in the archive.

The table is one checklist, in the order in which the record is read.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which change and which deltas the run answers, and the record follows them The run merges the delta of another change, or only some of the deltas the change holds
The delta merged is the delta of the change The main specification changed only where the change's delta names a requirement A requirement outside the delta changed, or one the delta names did not
Each operation did what the merge rules say Added requirements are present, a modified one carries the change and every scenario it had before, removed ones are gone, and a renamed one has the new name only A modified requirement lost a scenario, a removed one is still there, or a rename left both names
Nothing the delta did not mention changed The rest of the main specification is as it was, in its order A requirement was reworded or moved as a side effect
No delta heading remains The main specification has one ## Requirements section and no ## ADDED or other delta heading The delta file was copied in unchanged
The Purpose is not a placeholder A new capability carries the delta's own Purpose, and an existing one is unchanged A new specification carries the placeholder, or an existing Purpose was rewritten
validate passes on the main specifications The form of the run is the one the project uses, run on the files as they are now The result is from before the merge, or the run used a form that does not read the main specifications
The folder is in the archive under its date with every artifact The folder, with the proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks, is under archive The change was archived without its merge, or the folder lacks an artifact
The path and the skips are known Someone can say which path was used and what it skipped The record was made by a path nobody wrote down, with a check skipped
Downstream The next change starts from a record that a person has read The folder moved and no one read the main specification

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A change in the archive is a change that was moved. The main specification is what the next change relies on. So the record is accepted when someone has read the main specification, not when the folder has moved.

For both sync and archive, the developer can follow one routine:

  1. Commit the repository before the run, so that the merge and the move show as one diff.
  2. Read the delta first and say which requirements it changes, and decide the path and whether to sync before the archive.
  3. Answer each question the path asks as a decision, and note each check that was skipped.
  4. After the run, read the diff of openspec/specs/ beside the delta, operation by operation, and read each changed requirement whole.
  5. Run validate in the form the project uses, and read the whole result.
  6. Commit once the record is read, and name the path and the skipped checks in the message, because the archive does not keep them.

12.5 Changing the result

When the review finds that the record is wrong, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on whether the merge has happened.

What exists What the revision covers
The delta only, nothing merged An edit of the delta, by the ways of chapter 6, and then either path.
The sync run and the change open The same edit, and the sync again. The skill tells the agent to make the operation idempotent, so that a second run gives the result of one.
The change archived with a wrong requirement Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example shows the last row and none of the others. The first change was archived with a requirement that did not cover a case. The correction was a new change that modified it. Section 4.8 tells this story. Section 4.14 shows the main specification afterwards, with the first change's folder as it was. The example holds no other case. It runs no sync, so no change reached the main specification before it was archived, and no change is still open.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the main specification by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. The two differ in cost and in how they go wrong.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when One word or one block of the main specification is wrong and the developer knows the replacement. An example is a Purpose, which a delta cannot change for an existing capability The delta changed, or several requirements have to change together
What it costs The change records nothing of the edit, and a delta that modifies the block does not know about it Another merge, and a request that names the change and the deltas
How it goes wrong A later MODIFIED copies the old block, and the correction is lost An operation is not idempotent, or the run changes a requirement the delta does not name
What to check afterwards The diff of the main specification, and the delta of any active change that names the block The diff of the main specification against the new delta, and validate --specs

Suppose the developer corrects a word in the requirement of purchase by hand, in the main specification. A change that was drafted before the correction then modifies that requirement, and it copies the block from its own earlier draft. The merge replaces the block with the delta's block, and the correction is lost. The diff shows the old word coming back. Nothing in the program says that the word was ever corrected.

Suppose a delta is edited after a sync, and the sync is run again. The skill tells the agent to make the operation idempotent, so that two runs give the same result as one. No run was observed. The check that the main specification says what the new delta says is the developer's.

Both means are checked by reading the main specification, not only the diff. The diff shows words, and the main specification is what the next change relies on. A revision is read as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

12.6 What sync and archive pass on

Sync and archive pass a record to the next change. The main specification is the living description that chapter 3 spoke of. Section 4.14 says that archiving turns a change from a proposal into part of that description. The workflows of the last four chapters end here. The plan is written, carried out, checked and made current. The next change starts from the record, and its requirements are read against what the record holds.

Sync merges a delta without moving the change, and it exists only as a skill. Archive merges and moves the change. It exists as a command that does this in the program, and as a workflow that has the agent do it. The two paths differ in who merges and what is checked, and both can skip a check. The merge rules say what the main specification should hold. The review is of the main specification that the merge left, not of the folder that moved. Where the skill says two things about one operation, a delta can rely on the stricter one, which the program checks, and a modified requirement is written whole. The archive is a record, and a new change corrects a mistake in it. The question to ask of any archive is which path made the record and what it checked.

13. Customizing the Harness, and What the Tool Checks

The previous four chapters discussed the workflows of OpenSpec and what each one leaves behind. All of them depended on the default: the core profile or one workflow added to it, the schema spec-driven, and a configuration file with a few lines of context. This chapter is about changing that default. It names four kinds of customization and puts the possibilities that OpenSpec offers in one table. It asks four questions of each kind. Where is it made? What does it change? What does the tool check? How is it changed later? The example is the vending machine with a schema of its own. The next chapter builds that schema file by file.

13.1 Four kinds of customization, and the possibilities in one table

A project can change four things, and they differ in how far a change reaches. The profile decides which workflows are installed, and it belongs to the machine. The project configuration holds the default schema, text that is added to what the agent is told, and advice for apply and archive. It belongs to one project. The schema defines the artifacts of a change, what each one requires, and what the agent is told when it writes each one. It belongs to one project, and projects can share it. The instruction file, AGENTS.md, holds rules that the agent reads when a session opens. It is next to OpenSpec and is not part of it.

The first three are OpenSpec's own. Each of them is a file that the machine or the project controls. The fourth is named here because it is the fourth place where a rule can be written. Section 13.7 says why it is not in the table below.

The question to ask of a need is which kind it belongs to. A rule about the wording of one artifact belongs in the configuration. A new file that every change must have belongs in the schema. The choice of which workflows a person can call by name belongs in the profile. A rule for every task in the project, OpenSpec or not, belongs in the instruction file. The tool accepts the same text in more than one of them, and it does not say which place was right. The chapters before this one taught the default, and this chapter goes beyond it.

The table has one row for each file in which OpenSpec can be customized. So a possibility is found in the row of the file it is written in. The columns say which kind the file belongs to, how the file is made, what it holds, and what the tool checks. A cell that says "Nothing" means that no command reads it or reports on it. The fields of schema.yaml are those of the schema reference on openspec.dev. That reference lists every field, including the artifact's description and the apply block's instruction.

File Kind Made with What it holds What the tool checks
The global configuration Profile openspec config profile The profile and its workflow list openspec config list reports it, and openspec update writes the skills to match
openspec/config.yaml Config openspec init, then by hand schema; context; rules by artifact id; operations.apply.guidance; operations.archive.guidance; an opt-in for a hosted coding agent; store and references, for stores; skillsScope Read when instructions are fetched, and nothing about what the text says
schema.yaml Schema openspec schema fork or init, or by copying a folder The name, version and description; for each artifact its id, generates, description, template, instruction and requires, and their order; the apply block with requires, tracks and instruction openspec schema validate reports a syntax error, a missing template, a duplicate id and a cycle; openspec status shows a blocked artifact; nothing about the instruction texts, the order or apply.instruction
A file in templates/ Schema By hand, or copied with the schema The headings and comments the agent starts from openspec schema validate reports a missing file, and nothing about its content
.openspec.yaml of a change Schema openspec new change; --schema sets it The schema that change uses openspec status reports it

A schema has one more place besides the project's openspec/schemas/<name>/ folder. That place is the user's data directory, where every project on the machine finds it. The file is the same in both places. Section 13.4 says how openspec schema which tells the two places apart. A schema written by someone else is copied into either place, and it is then checked like any other schema. The seven community schemas that the customization page lists are examples.

13.2 The profile: which workflows exist

The profile is the customization that reaches furthest and is checked least. It decides which workflows are installed as skills, and so which ones a person can ask for. Chapter 9 defines the profile and names the six workflows of the core profile. This section adds one point: the profile is not a setting of the project. It is set with openspec config profile, and openspec config has only the global scope. So a person who sets it changes it for every project on the machine. The program reminds the person to run openspec update in each project, because the skills are rewritten only then.

A project that wants a profile of its own has no setting for it. The way to get one is to keep a separate configuration directory and to start the session with that directory named. The program then reads the profile from there and from nowhere else. This repository does this, and its profile adds the continue workflow to the core six. The profile has one retired field, delivery, which 2.1.1 reads and ignores. Where the skills are installed is a second choice with the same reach. From release 2.1, openspec init puts them in the machine's ~/.agents/skills/ unless it is given --scope project. A project that keeps its own skills records that in its configuration, as this repository does.

The tool reports the result in openspec config list. It does not say whether the installed workflows suit the project. A person who is in the wrong directory gets the global profile without a warning.

13.3 The project configuration: text that is added, and none of it enforced

The project configuration is a file, openspec/config.yaml. openspec init creates it with commented examples of context, rules and operations. It does four things.

It names the default schema, so a new change needs no flag. It holds context, which is added to the instruction of every artifact. It holds rules, which are added to the instruction of the artifact whose id matches. So a rule about the design is read when the design is written, and at no other time. And it holds advice for apply and archive, in operations. This advice is kept apart from the rules, because it describes how the work is done and not what an artifact contains.

When the agent asks for the instruction of an artifact, the program returns the schema's instruction with the context, the rules and the template, each in its own field. The agent asks for the apply and archive instructions in the same way. It gets context and operationGuidance as fields of their own. The command that returns the archive instruction only reads. In the scratch project it wrote no file, and its answer held the change's name, the root, the context and the guidance. The customization page says that context is a required input to the prompt and that guidance is additive. The same page says that neither is enforceable. A workflow follows the entries that apply and reports a conflict. It copies none of the text into a file unless the person asks.

One key of the file is about files and not about the prompt. It is the opt-in for two files that let one hosted coding agent run OpenSpec: a workflow file and an agent file. When the key is true, openspec update writes them and keeps them current. When it is false, openspec update removes the ones it generated. When it is absent, the choice is undecided and update writes nothing. A second key is about files too. skillsScope: project says that the project keeps OpenSpec's skills in the repository. So openspec update refreshes them there and does not ask where to keep them.

The archive and sync workflows read one more thing, the specs rules, before they write a merge into a main specification. They stop if the lookup fails. That is the one place where the configuration is read for something that is not a prompt.

Of all this, the tool checks the file, which it reads. It checks nothing about what a rule says or whether an agent followed it. A context that is wrong is injected in the same way as one that is right.

13.4 Which schema a change uses

Four places decide which schema a change uses, and the tool reads them in order. The --schema flag on the command that creates the change comes first. Next comes the schema that the change itself recorded, in the .openspec.yaml of its folder. Then comes the default named in the configuration. Last comes the default of the program, spec-driven.

A new change writes its own schema into its .openspec.yaml when it is created, and that record outranks the default in the configuration. In the scratch project, a change was created under a fork, and its .openspec.yaml was then edited by hand. After that, the change reported spec-driven as its schema, though the configuration still named the fork.

When a schema is not the one a person expects, openspec schema which says where it comes from. It reports the schema's name, its Source and its Path. With --all it lists the project schemas, the user schemas and the schemas of the package. A project schema outranks a user schema of the same name. The customization page recommends project schemas, because they are kept with the code.

13.5 Building a schema

A schema is a folder, openspec/schemas/<name>/, that holds one file, schema.yaml, and a templates/ folder. There are two ways to start. A fork copies an existing schema whole, so the project starts from spec-driven and removes or adds artifacts. A new schema starts from nothing except the artifacts that are named. In the scratch project, a schema of two artifacts was written: the proposal and the tasks, neither of them requiring anything, and an apply block that requires and tracks the tasks. The command openspec schema init with no option writes four artifacts, each with a template: the proposal, the specs, the design and the tasks. It writes the same kind of apply block. One option names a different list of artifacts, and another makes the new schema the project's default.

The file has five top-level keys: the name, a version, a description, the list of artifacts, and the apply block. Each artifact has an id, the file it generates, a description, the template it starts from, the instruction it gives the agent, and the artifacts it requires. The table of section 13.1 lists these fields.

The fields differ in what they decide. requires decides what is possible. An artifact whose required artifacts do not exist is blocked, and openspec status says which ones block it. An artifact counts as done when its generated file exists. In the scratch project, a change whose design file was empty was reported as complete. The order of the list decides only which artifact comes first when several are ready. A template is Markdown that is injected into the prompt. It may hold headings, comments with guidance and a sample. generates may be a pattern, and this is how the default schema writes one file for each capability. The apply block says which artifact must exist before apply, and which file's boxes are counted. Its instruction is what openspec instructions apply returns while the change is ready. When the change is blocked or every task is done, the program writes its own text, and the schema's instruction does not appear.

openspec schema validate checks that the file is well formed. In the scratch project it reported a missing template file, an artifact id that was used twice, and a cycle of requirements, which it named. The customization page lists the same four checks: the syntax, the templates, the cycles and the ids.

A schema is shared by copying its folder. A schema in the user's data directory is available to every project on the machine. The customization page lists seven schemas that others wrote and that are not part of the core. A schema copied from elsewhere is a fork of it. A fork does not receive later changes to the schema it was copied from. The project keeps it up to date by hand, or not at all. This repository's own schema is of this kind: it has no specs, and its design carries a chapter outline.

13.6 Where the needs of an example belong

The next chapter follows one example from the first command to the archive. This section only says where its needs belong. Chapter 4 told how the first version of the vending machine passed validation and every task, and still left a case undecided. The design had named the case as a non-goal. Chapter 7 said that a design that sets a case aside has not decided it. The review that finds this is a habit of the reviewer, and nothing in the tool knows whether it was done. The example makes the habit a file. The file is a fork of spec-driven, named with-trace. Its trace names, for every scenario, the decision in the design that satisfies it.

The example needs four things, and each one belongs in a different place. The table says where and why.

The need Where it is made Why there
A file that every change must have before its tasks The schema: the trace artifact, and requires on the tasks It is a new artifact with its own place in the order, and only the schema can add one.
A design states a non-goal only when no scenario tests the case The configuration: a line in rules for the design It is about the wording of one artifact, and not about a file.
The agent checks the trace before each task The schema: a line in apply.instruction It belongs with the trace and is copied with the schema, so another project that copies the schema gets it.
The archive summary says whether the trace was read before the merge The configuration: a line of archive guidance It is advice about how the work is done, and it is for this project.

Of such a customization, the tool checks the form. It reports the schema as valid and the trace as blocked or ready. It does not check that the trace is true, or that the line in the apply instruction is followed. It cannot find a scenario that nobody wrote. The first version failed on a case that had no scenario until the second change added it. So the trace would have made the design's non-goal visible once the scenario existed. The coverage review of chapter 6 remains the check that finds a missing scenario. The example is also a fork. It keeps nothing of later changes to spec-driven, so the project that keeps it maintains the copy by hand.

13.7 What is outside OpenSpec

The instruction file is the fourth place where a rule can be written, and OpenSpec has no mechanism for it. The agent reads AGENTS.md when a session opens, and the program does not read it. In 2.1.1 the program treats it as something to leave alone. The program's cleanup code treats two things as left by earlier versions: a managed openspec/AGENTS.md, and a block of text between two markers in the root AGENTS.md. In the scratch project, the project still had both. openspec init removed the managed file and the marked block, and it kept the rest of the root file as the person had written it. openspec update alone changed neither. The root file belongs to the project, and nothing in OpenSpec generates, reads or checks it.

That is why it is not a row of the table. The last column of the table says what the tool checks. A row that says "Nothing" about a file the tool does not know would suggest that the tool does something with it. It is better compared with the project configuration, which is the place nearest to it.

AGENTS.md The configuration's context and rules
Read by The agent, when a session opens The agent, added to the instruction of an OpenSpec artifact or operation
Applies to Every task in the project, OpenSpec or not Only the artifacts and operations OpenSpec instructs
What the tool checks Nothing The file's form, and nothing about what it says

A rule that every task must follow belongs in the instruction file. The language of the project's files is such a rule. A rule about what one artifact contains belongs in the configuration, where it is read when the artifact is written. A rule written in both places can disagree with itself, and nothing warns of it. So the person who writes both has to read them together. Section 3.5 gave the reason why the rules are kept with the code. This chapter adds only that they are in two places, and that the tool knows one of them.

13.8 What the tool checks, and what it does not check

The tool checks the form of a customization and never its effect. openspec config list reports the profile. The configuration is read as a file. The schema is checked for its syntax, its templates, its cycles and its ids. The instruction file is not checked at all.

The effect is left to the reviewer, and it can fail in ways that the checks do not see. A schema that validates can tell the agent something that does not produce the artifact that the template holds. The default schema already does this once: section 7.7 shows that its instruction for the design names two parts that the template lacks. A rule can be ignored, because it is advice that the agent reads. A context can be wrong, and it is injected as it is. The guidance for apply and archive is advisory, and no command reports whether it was followed. The order of the artifact list and the wording of a fork's instruction change what an agent does. Nothing checks them.

Each of these can happen to a change that passes every command. So a customization that is reported as well-formed has shown that it is well-formed, and no more.

13.9 Reviewing a customization

A customization is reviewed first in the file and then in what it produces. The review has four passes. Placement asks whether the need is at the kind that reaches as far as it should. Form asks whether the tool accepts the customization. Instruction asks whether each instruction produces the part that the template holds. Effect asks whether a change run through the schema produces what was meant. Placement and Effect matter most. The tool can check Form and nothing else, and a customization at the wrong kind or with the wrong effect passes that check.

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it.

Check The customization has done its job when How it can fail
Placement The need is at the kind that reaches as far as the need, and no further A rule for one artifact is in the instruction file, or a rule for every task is in the rules of one artifact
The profile openspec config list shows the workflows the project needs The wrong configuration directory was used, and the global profile was read
The configuration openspec instructions returns the context and the rules for the artifact they were written for A rule is under an id that no artifact has
The schema's form openspec schema validate passes and openspec schema which names the intended source A project schema shadows a user schema of the same name, or the reverse
The selection A new change records the schema that was meant A flag or a default is set that overrides it
The instruction Each instruction produces the part the template holds An instruction names a part the template does not have
The effect A change run through the schema produces the artifacts that were meant, and they are good The schema validates and the artifacts are wrong

13.10 Changing a customization

The cost of changing a customization depends on what has already been made with it. The table says what the revision covers in each case.

What exists What the revision covers
Nothing has been made with it yet The file only. The next command that reads it sees the change.
Active changes A configuration edit is read the next time the instructions are fetched. A schema edited in place changes the active changes that use it at once: in the scratch project, a change created with four artifacts reported five after the schema gained one, and the new one was blocked. A change keeps the schema name it recorded, so a new default does not move it. A profile change reaches the skills only after openspec update.
Changes archived Nothing. The archive is a record and is not rewritten, as chapters 5 and 12 say. A change made under the old schema stays as it was made, and the next change uses the new one.

The row for active changes is the one to read most carefully. Every change that names a schema shares it, so an edit to the schema moves them all. A change that was half-written under one set of artifacts then finds another set. A person who wants a change to keep the old schema copies the schema under a new name before editing it. That person then starts the new changes with the copy.

13.11 What customization passes on

Customization passes to the project a harness of its own. The profile says which workflows can be called. The configuration says what is added to what the agent is told. The schema says what a change is made of. Each is a file that is kept with the project or the machine, and each can be read, reviewed and revised like any other file. The tool accepts all of it when it is well formed, and it says nothing about whether it was wise.

A customization is a choice of the kind that reaches as far as the need and no further, and the tool confirms only that it was made well-formed. The question to ask of any customization is where it was made and what is checked there.

14. A Customized Change, from Fork to Archive

The previous chapter said what can be customized, and what the tool checks for each kind of customization. This chapter shows it in practice. It uses the vending machine's second change, refuse-without-exact-change, which chapter 4 quotes in full. The chapter makes this change again under a schema of its own, with-trace. The schema adds one artifact, a trace, between the design and the tasks. The chapter shows every file that the customization adds or changes. It also shows the console input and the main output of each step. The proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks of the change are chapter 4's. This chapter points to them and does not repeat them. The table of section 13.6 lists the four needs of the example and the place where each need is met.

The walkthrough ran on OpenSpec 2.1.1 in a scratch project on 20 November 2026. The scratch project starts from the machine's own configuration and from a main specification that holds the first change's result. This chapter is the only one in the book that shows console blocks. Its claims are what the program printed, and a reader can check them only by seeing that output. A line that begins with $ is input, and the lines after it are the program's output. The project's folder is written as ., and the program's own install folder as <package>. A line of three dots marks output that is cut. No block shows the work of an agent. The files were written by hand in the scratch project.

14.1 Preparing the harness

The harness is prepared in four steps: a fork, a schema that differs from it, a template, and a configuration that names the fork. After each step, the program is asked what it now knows.

The scratch project holds the machine's own config.yaml, which names spec-driven. It also holds a main specification of purchase with the first change's result. So the project is the example's second change, waiting to be made. The first of the four steps is the fork. It copies the package's spec-driven into the project under a new name.

$ openspec schema fork spec-driven with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
- Forking 'spec-driven' to 'with-trace'...
✔ Forked 'spec-driven' to 'with-trace'

Source: <package>/schemas/spec-driven (package)
Destination: ./openspec/schemas/with-trace

You can now customize the schema at:
  ./openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml

openspec schema which says where a schema comes from. With --all, it lists the schemas that the project can reach. The fork is a project schema, and spec-driven is still the package's schema.

$ openspec schema which with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
Schema: with-trace
Source: project
Path: ./openspec/schemas/with-trace
$ openspec schema which --all
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.

Project schemas:
  with-trace

Package schemas:
  spec-driven

The second step is to edit schema.yaml in the new folder. The file is the package's default of 273 lines, so the chapter shows it as the difference from the fork. The diff has four changes. The description says what the fork is. A trace artifact is added after the design, and it requires the specs and the design. The tasks gain trace in their requires. The apply block gains two lines. The lines of the default schema that the diff does not show are unchanged.

--- a/openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml
+++ b/openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 name: with-trace
 version: 1
-description: Default OpenSpec workflow - proposal → specs → design → tasks
+description: spec-driven with a trace between the design and the tasks
 artifacts:
   - id: proposal
     generates: proposal.md
@@ -196,6 +196,22 @@ artifacts:
     requires:
       - proposal

+  - id: trace
+    generates: trace.md
+    description: Which decision in the design satisfies each scenario
+    template: trace.md
+    instruction: |
+      Create the trace that names, for every scenario in the specs, the decision in
+      the design that satisfies it.
+
+      Write one row for each scenario, using the scenario's own name. Walk the
+      scenario's inputs through the design by hand. If the design has no decision
+      that covers the scenario, write "none" and record the scenario as not
+      satisfied; do not edit the design to hide the gap.
+    requires:
+      - specs
+      - design
+
   - id: tasks
     generates: tasks.md
     description: Implementation checklist with trackable tasks
@@ -264,6 +280,7 @@ artifacts:
     requires:
       - specs
       - design
+      - trace

 apply:
   requires: [ tasks ]
@@ -271,3 +288,5 @@ apply:
   instruction: |
     Read context files, work through pending tasks, mark complete as you go.
     Pause if you hit blockers or need clarification.
+    Before each task, read trace.md and stop if a scenario the task touches is
+    marked not satisfied.

The requires of the trace puts it between the design and the tasks. The requires of the tasks makes it mandatory. The two lines of the apply block are the third of the example's four needs. The third step is the template that the trace's template: trace.md names. It is a new file, templates/trace.md, in the same folder. The block below shows the whole file.

## Trace

<!-- One row for every scenario in the specs. Name the decision in the design that
     satisfies the scenario. A scenario with no decision is written as "none" and is
     not satisfied. -->

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| <!-- scenario name --> | <!-- decision, or none --> | <!-- yes or no --> |

The fourth step is openspec/config.yaml. The configuration needs three changes. It names the fork as the default schema. It gains a rule for the design, which is the example's second need. It also gains a line of archive guidance, which is the fourth need. The machine's own context and its rule for the tasks stay as they were.

--- a/openspec/config.yaml
+++ b/openspec/config.yaml
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-schema: spec-driven
+schema: with-trace

 context: |
   This OpenSpec root holds one example for the book in
@@ -15,6 +15,13 @@ context: |
   is replaced rather than defended.

 rules:
+  design:
+    - State a case as a non-goal only if no scenario tests it.
   tasks:
     - Each task states how it is verified, by reading the artifacts or by running
       `openspec validate`.
+
+operations:
+  archive:
+    guidance:
+      - The archive summary says whether trace.md was read before the merge.

Then the program is asked whether the schema is well formed. Section 13.5 says what this check covers: the syntax, the template files, the ids and the cycles.

$ openspec schema validate with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
✓ Schema 'with-trace' is valid

The answer says that the schema is valid. It says nothing about the instruction of the trace, and that instruction is the new part that matters.

14.2 A new change uses the new default schema

A new change needs no flag, because the configuration now names the fork. The program says which schema it used. It also writes that schema into the change's own file.

$ openspec new change refuse-without-exact-change
- Creating change 'refuse-without-exact-change' with schema 'with-trace'...
Created change 'refuse-without-exact-change' at openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change/
Schema: with-trace
Next: openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change

So far, the change's folder holds one file, .openspec.yaml. From now on, this file is the record that outranks the configuration's default (section 13.4).

schema: with-trace
created: 2026-11-20

openspec status lists the artifacts and what blocks each one. There are five artifacts, not four. The trace is blocked until both the specs and the design exist.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 0/5 artifacts complete

[ ] proposal
[-] specs (blocked by: proposal)
[-] design (blocked by: proposal)
[-] trace (blocked by: specs, design)
[-] tasks (blocked by: specs, design, trace)

Next: openspec instructions proposal --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

The order of the first three artifacts is the one that chapters 3 and 4 gave. The customization changed the end. The tasks waited for the specs and the design, and now they wait for the trace as well.

14.3 What the agent is told

The schema and the configuration decide what the agent is told when it asks for an artifact or an operation. The program shows this as JSON. The three commands below are the ones whose output carries the customization. The output is long, so each block is cut to the field that the customization put there.

The design's instruction is the schema's. The configuration's context, rules and template are each in a field of their own. The rule for the design is the one that the fourth step of section 14.1 wrote.

$ openspec instructions design --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "rules": [
    "State a case as a non-goal only if no scenario tests it."
  ],
...
}

The archive's guidance is a field of its own. It is not a rule, as section 13.3 said.

$ openspec instructions archive --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "operationGuidance": [
    "The archive summary says whether trace.md was read before the merge."
  ],
...
}

The apply instruction is the schema's. It appears in the output once the change is ready, and section 14.6 reaches that point. What it says is the two lines that the diff added. What the program prints is what the agent is told. The program does not show whether an agent follows it.

14.4 The trace, the new file

The proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks of the change are chapter 4's. They are written as chapter 4 quotes them. Once the proposal exists, specs and design are ready, and the trace waits for both. After the design, the program says that the trace is next. It also says that the tasks wait only for the trace.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 3/5 artifacts complete

[x] proposal
[x] specs
[x] design
[ ] trace
[-] tasks (blocked by: trace)

Next: openspec instructions trace --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

The trace is written from the design's Findings, where chapter 4 quotes Traces B, C and D. No archive holds this file. So it is written for this chapter, as the previous chapter's example was, and it is not the output of an agent run. Its three rows are the three scenarios of the delta. Each row names the decision in the design that satisfies the scenario.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| Change is given from stock | Work out the change before the product is released; 30 owed is 20 and 10 (Trace C) | yes |
| Exact payment gives no change | Nothing is owed, so the change is exact and no coin is returned (Trace D) | yes |
| Stock cannot make the change | If the change is not exact, refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the amount inserted (Trace B) | yes |

With the trace written, the tasks are ready. When the tasks are written, the program reports all five artifacts.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete

[x] proposal
[x] specs
[x] design
[x] trace
[x] tasks

All planning artifacts complete!
Next: openspec instructions apply --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

14.5 What the trace would have shown about the first design

The trace was added because of what the first version failed to do. Chapter 4 told that story. The design of give-exact-change set the stock case aside as a non-goal. The change passed validation and every task. A walkthrough written afterwards found the case undecided. The question here is where the trace would have shown the problem.

The file below is a trace of the first design, against the three scenarios of the second change. It is hypothetical, and it is written for this chapter. The machine did not write it. The first change did not have the scenario that the trace lists last. The first two rows follow the first design's own Findings, and the third row follows its Non-Goals.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| Change is given from stock | Work out the change greedily from the stock; 30 owed is 20 and 10 | yes |
| Exact payment gives no change | Nothing is owed, so no coin is returned | yes |
| Stock cannot make the change | none | no |

The third row has no decision. The trace's instruction tells whoever writes it to say so, and not to edit the design to hide the gap. The configuration's rule would have found the same row from the other side. The first design states exactly that case as a non-goal, while a scenario now tests it.

This is a limit as well as a finding. The row exists because the scenario exists. The first change had no scenario for the stock case. So a trace of it would have had two rows, and both would have read yes. A trace finds a scenario that has no decision. It cannot find a scenario that nobody wrote. That is the coverage review of chapter 6, and the trace does not replace it. The trace does not prevent the failure either. It puts the failure where the review is cheapest: after the design and before the first task.

14.6 Apply, validate and archive

Apply reads the tasks. While the tasks are unticked, the program returns the schema's instruction. The boxes of chapter 4's tasks are ticked in the archive. So the scratch project's copy has them unticked, and it ticks them after this command, as an apply would. The output is cut to the fields that matter.

$ openspec instructions apply --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "state": "ready",
  "instruction": "Read context files, work through pending tasks, mark complete as you go.\nPause if you hit blockers or need clarification.\nBefore each task, read trace.md and stop if a scenario the task touches is\nmarked not satisfied.",
...
}

The last two lines are the diff's. The program returns them, and it counts nothing about whether they are followed. With the boxes ticked, validate passes the change.

$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

The command checks the structure of the specifications. It does not open the trace, and a trace that is a row of dashes passes it. The next block is a run and not advice. The trace is replaced by a one-row placeholder, and status and validate are run again.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| - | - | - |

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete
...
$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

The program counts an artifact by its file. It counts the placeholder like the table of three rows, because the file is there. Then the original trace is restored, and archive is run.

$ openspec archive refuse-without-exact-change --yes
Task status: ✓ Complete

Specs to update:
  purchase: update
Applying changes to openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md:
  ~ 1 modified
Totals: + 0, ~ 1, - 0, → 0
Specs updated successfully.
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' archived as '2026-11-20-refuse-without-exact-change'.

The command moves the whole folder, as chapter 12 said. The archived folder holds the trace beside the design.

$ ls openspec/changes/archive/2026-11-20-refuse-without-exact-change/
design.md
proposal.md
specs
tasks.md
trace.md

The guidance for the archive asked the summary to say whether the trace was read. The archive command writes no summary, and the output above has none. Such a summary would be written in the archive workflow, which the agent runs. Nothing checks that the summary says it.

14.7 What the customization costs

The customization costs a fork, and one more file for every change. The fork is a copy of spec-driven as it was on the day it was made. Nothing flows from the package into it. So the project keeps it up to date by hand, or does not keep it up to date. Every change carries one more artifact. That is one more file to write after the design, and to read before the first task.

What the tool counts is not what was reviewed. A design edited after the trace leaves the trace as it was. The next line is appended to the design of the scratch change. It is a decision that the trace does not mention. Then status and validate are asked what they report.

**Decision**: refuse every purchase for which the stock holds fewer than three coins.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete
...
$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

Five of five, and valid, after a decision that the trace never traced. The trace is as good as the review that wrote it and the review that reads it. The program knows about neither review.

A customized change is the default change with one more file. The program shows that the file exists, that the schema is well formed, and what each instruction says. It shows nothing about whether the trace is true, or whether it was read before the tasks. It also shows nothing about whether the summary at the archive said so. Those questions stay with the reviewer, as the previous chapter said of every customization.

15. The Workflows Outside the Table

Chapters 9 to 12 examined seven workflows and one command in detail, and gave each a card and a table of its stages. These are the workflows of one profile. OpenSpec 2.1.1 defines five more. This chapter discusses all five in one place. It gives each a short section in place of a card and a table. Each section answers the questions that chapter 9 asks of a workflow. A reader who wants the stages of a skill reads the skill. The skill is a text in the project's skills folder.

15.1 Five more workflows

The program holds a longer list of workflows than the seven that chapter 9 tables. In OpenSpec 2.1.1 the list has twelve entries: propose, explore, new, continue, apply, update, ff, sync, archive, bulk-archive, verify and onboard.

A project whose profile names all twelve gets twelve skills. A scratch project showed this on 20 November 2026, on 2.1.1. There, openspec init --scope project with a global profile that listed all twelve installed twelve skills in the project's skills folder. This repository's profile names seven, so the repository has seven skills. The table of chapter 9 is the table of that profile. It is not wrong because it is shorter than the program's list.

The table lists the five workflows outside it. The text calls one of them Fast-forward. The program's name for it is ff.

Workflow Entry point What it does
New the skill openspec-new-change Create a change and show the template of its first artifact, then stop.
Fast-forward the skill openspec-ff-change Create all of a change's planning artifacts in one run.
Verify the skill openspec-verify-change Compare the implementation with the change's artifacts and report what does not match.
Bulk-archive the skill openspec-bulk-archive-change Archive several changes in one run, after checking their deltas against each other.
Onboard the skill openspec-onboard Guide the developer through one whole change, on a real task, with narration.

None of the five writes a kind of file that the workflows of the table do not write. New and fast-forward write the artifacts that propose and continue write. Verify writes nothing. Bulk-archive moves what archive moves. Onboard writes the artifacts, the code and the archive. The five differ in two things: how much is written or moved in one run, and how much the agent is told to ask.

15.2 New

The skill openspec-new-change starts a change and writes nothing into it. If the request does not say what the developer wants to build, the skill asks. It derives a name in lowercase with hyphens and creates the change. It shows the change's status and the template of the first artifact, and then it stops. It is the first half of the path that chapter 10 describes, and continue is the second half. New creates the place, and each run of continue fills one artifact.

The agent asks and runs commands, and the program creates the folder and reports the state. The skill passes no schema unless the developer names one or asks to see them. So the project's default schema is used. In a scratch project on the default schema, new change created a folder that held .openspec.yaml. This file has the schema's name and the date of creation. status then showed zero of four artifacts complete. The proposal was ready, and the other three were blocked.

The program refuses three things, each with an error and exit code 1: a name already in use, a name that is not in lowercase with hyphens, and a schema it does not have. Two other things also stop the skill: a request that the agent cannot turn into a name, and a project with no root.

A reviewer judges a run of new by what is missing: the folder holds .openspec.yaml and no artifact. The developer says what the change is for. The developer names a schema if the default is not wanted. The developer also decides when the first artifact is written, and by which workflow.

15.3 Fast-forward

The skill openspec-ff-change creates a change and writes every artifact in its required set in one run. Propose does the same, and the two skills are close. Fast-forward has five numbered stages and propose has seven. The loop that writes the artifacts is the same text in both skills, with two exceptions: a tick mark in the progress line, and the word "critically" before "unclear". Section 10.2 gives the stages of propose and what the program checks at each.

Fast-forward leaves out what surrounds the loop. It does not clarify the request before anything is written, it does not load the project's context, and it does not choose a schema. Three differences follow.

  • Fast-forward passes no schema, so the developer can choose another schema only in the request.
  • It asks only when the context is critically unclear, and otherwise it prefers reasonable decisions. Propose asks about an ambiguity that would change the scope, the observable behaviour, the compatibility or the acceptance criteria. Propose also tells the agent to record a minor assumption in the artifacts. The skill of fast-forward has no sentence that tells the agent to record one.
  • Propose opens with a paragraph that says the request authorises planning only, and that tells the agent to stop. Fast-forward has no such paragraph. Both skills close with the same prompt. The prompt calls the plan ready for review and offers to apply it when the developer asks.

The skill says nothing about the boundary. That is a difference in the text, and not a defect found in a run.

The agent writes. The program supplies the build order, and the template and instruction of each artifact. A reviewer reads a run in the way chapter 10 reads a run of propose. The required set exists or was reported as skipped, and nothing outside the change's folder was edited. The developer's part has two additions. First, say in the request that the run is for planning and not for building, because the skill does not say it. Second, look for assumptions in the drafts, because nothing marks them, and an unmarked assumption reads as a decision.

15.4 Verify

The skill openspec-verify-change compares the implementation with the change's artifacts and reports the result. It selects the change. It asks the program for the status and for the apply instruction. The apply instruction returns the artifact files, the tasks and the count of tasks that are done. The skill then reads the artifacts and checks three dimensions:

  • Completeness counts the tasks and looks for each requirement in the code.
  • Correctness reads each requirement and each scenario of the delta and looks for an implementation and for a test.
  • Coherence compares the implementation with the decisions of the design and with the patterns of the project.

Each finding is critical, a warning or a suggestion. When the agent is uncertain, the skill tells it to prefer the lower severity. A removed requirement is checked in the inverse way, so the expected result is that no implementation is found. A renamed requirement is checked for the behaviour it kept.

The skill marks a check that the schema does not define as not applicable. It marks a check whose evidence is missing as not verified. It never scores a skipped check as a pass. It says "ready for archive" only when nothing is critical and no check was skipped.

The program contributes the files and the counts. The agent makes the comparison, by searching the code for keywords and by reasoning. The skill describes a report. It tells the agent not to implement tasks or archive the change while it verifies. It names no file to write. It says that the report is advisory and that archive keeps its own checks.

A reviewer judges a report by its evidence. Each finding should name a file and a line, and a clean report is as good as its search. The developer reads the report as advice, and decides what a finding means for the artifacts and for the code. Two further questions are separate: what a passing report shows, and what to do with a mismatch. This chapter does not answer them.

15.5 Bulk-archive

The skill openspec-bulk-archive-change archives several changes in one run. It lists the active changes and asks the developer to choose among them, with an option for all. It never chooses for the developer. For each chosen change, it collects the status of the artifacts, the count of tasks, the delta files, and the name that the archive folder would have. It marks a change as blocked if the change's archive folder already exists.

The skill then looks for a conflict. A conflict is two chosen changes with deltas for the same capability. The skill settles a conflict by looking in the code for what each change implemented:

  • If only one is implemented, it syncs that one.
  • If both are, it applies them oldest first, so that the newer overwrites.
  • If neither is, it skips the sync and warns.
