It shows one table of all the changes with their artifacts, tasks, deltas and conflicts. It asks one question, with three options: archive all, archive only the ready ones, or cancel. After a yes, it fetches the rules of the specifications and syncs the included deltas of each change inline. It checks the main specifications against the deltas, and only then moves the change's folder. If a target folder has appeared in the meantime, that change fails and the batch does not. At the end, the skill reports every outcome.

The agent does the merging and the moving, and the program supplies the lists, the statuses and the counts. This is the path of chapter 12 in which the agent merges, run over several changes.

The rule that settles a conflict asks for evidence in the code. So in a project whose changes are prose, the rule has nothing to find. A reviewer should read how each conflict was settled, and not trust the table's statement that it was settled. The developer chooses the changes, reads the table and gives the one confirmation. This confirmation is the only question the skill asks before it writes. Two further questions are separate: what a collision between two changes is, and what to do before the second archive. This chapter does not answer them. Chapter 16 discusses both questions, this one and the one at the end of section 15.4.

15.6 Onboard

The skill openspec-onboard is the longest of the twelve. In the scratch project it has 551 lines, against 87 for new and 128 for fast-forward. Most of its text is not an instruction to the program. It is text for the agent to say, in a fixed order, while the agent does a whole change with the developer on a real task in the project.

It begins with a preflight, which runs openspec --version and stops if the program is missing. It then continues in eleven stages: a welcome, the choice of a task, a short exploration, the creation of the change, the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks, then the implementation, the archive and a recap. To find the task, it scans the code for six things: comments that mark work to do, errors that are swallowed, functions without tests, loose types, debugging output, and user input that is not validated. It shows the developer three or four suggestions.

The skill marks four pauses: after the exploration, after the proposal draft, after the tasks draft, and before the implementation. It shows the proposal and the tasks as drafts, and saves each after approval. It marks no pause between the draft of the specification and the draft of the design. It implements in the codebase. It archives with openspec archive and the flag --yes. The skill says that this flag answers the confirmation prompts, which the skill cannot answer from a tool call. The developer may say that they need to stop. Then the skill tells the agent to say that the change is saved, and to point at openspec status for the state of the change. It also tells the agent to offer one next step from the workflows that the session has.

The agent teaches and does the work, and the program answers the commands that the skill calls. The skill itself says that it does real work in the developer's codebase. Nothing in it makes the work a sandbox. The change is a change of the project, the code is the project's code, and the archive is the project's archive.

A reviewer therefore judges onboard by what a project keeps: the diff of the code, the archived folder and the main specification. The reviewer asks of each one whether the developer would have accepted it without the tutorial. The developer chooses the task, approves the drafts at the pauses, confirms before the implementation, and says when to stop. Some repositories have rules that a change writes the book and not the code, or the code and not the book. In such a repository, the tutorial's change has to follow those rules too, because the skill does not know them.

15.7 Judging the results, and correcting them

The program sees the same things for all five workflows: which files exist and how many tasks are counted. It does not see who asked for a write or which assumption a draft holds. It does not see whether a pause was kept, whether a conflict was settled correctly, or whether a verify report is correct. The review of section 10.6 applies to each workflow. The evidence it adds is the table or the report that the skill shows at its end.

The cost of a wrong result differs by workflow:

  • A change that new started holds nothing the developer wrote. So the cheapest correction is to remove the folder and start again.
  • A result of fast-forward is revised by the paths of section 10.7. Its usual defect is an unrecorded assumption.
  • A verify report changes no file. So a wrong report costs a second run and a closer reading.
  • A bulk-archive run that went wrong has moved folders and merged specifications. So the last row of the table of section 10.7 applies to each change it archived: the archive holds no revision, and the correction is a new change.
  • The same holds for onboard. Its code is corrected by the project's own means, and the archive keeps its change as it was. A developer who stopped onboard early has an active change that continue and apply can work on further, and nothing to correct in the archive.

The five workflows outside the table add no kind of file and no check that the program makes. They differ in how much is written or moved in one run, and in how much the agent is told to ask. New writes no artifact. Fast-forward writes every artifact with fewer questions and no stated boundary. Verify writes nothing and reports. Bulk-archive moves several changes after one question. Onboard writes a whole change and the code with it. The program sees only that files exist and that tasks are counted. So the same thing separates a good run from a bad one in all five: the developer's reading of what was written or moved, who asked for it, and what it assumed. Of the five, only bulk-archive and onboard change the record of the project beyond a plan. A developer chooses either of them by what the project will keep.

16. What No Check Compares

Chapter 15 ended two of its sections on a question it did not answer. Section 15.4 left open what a passing verify report shows, and what to do with a mismatch. Section 15.5 left open what a collision between two changes is, and what to do before the second archive. Both questions ask about a comparison. In both cases, the tool does not make it. The first compares the specification with the code. The second compares two changes with each other. This chapter discusses the two together, because both depend on the same fact about the tool's checks. It does not introduce verify or bulk-archive again. Sections 15.4 and 15.5 do that. This chapter adds only what they leave open.

16.1 Three statements that are easy to confuse

It is easy to treat three statements about a change as one:

  • The change is well formed against the main specification.
  • Two changes that are open at the same time agree with each other.
  • The code does what a scenario of the specification says.

Chapters 11 and 12 showed how the first is checked. validate reads a change's delta and the main specifications. Archive checks the delta again before it merges it. Nothing in those chapters checks the second or the third. The rest of this chapter shows three things: why the first does not cover the other two, what the two workflows outside the profile add, and what the developer does instead.

16.2 What every check compares

Every check the tool makes compares one change with the main specifications. A scratch project on OpenSpec 2.1.1 showed this on 20 November 2026. It had one main requirement with one scenario. Two changes modified the wording of that requirement. One added the words "from its stock", and the other added "and notes". Both carried every scenario that the main specification had. Each change passed validate --strict on its own. Both passed validate --changes --strict in one run. list showed both as complete. No output named the overlap.

The other commands are the same. status takes one change by name, or all of them with --all. It has no option that relates two changes. A change's metadata file .openspec.yaml holds the schema and the date of creation. In a change that declares no spec changes, it also holds skip_specs. It has no field that names another change. So a pass says that a change is well formed against the main specification as it stands when the check runs. It says nothing about the main specification as it will stand after another change has been archived.

None of the checks reads code either. Chapter 11 says what validate reads, and chapter 12 says what archive reads. Neither is code. instructions apply counts the ticked boxes. Once every box is ticked, it tells the agent to review or verify the change before archiving, as section 8.5 says. It leaves the comparison with the code to whoever does the verifying.

16.3 Between two changes, the order of archiving decides

When two active changes modify the same requirement, the change archived second decides what the main specification holds. A modified requirement replaces the whole requirement, as chapter 6 says. Whether the tool allows the second archive depends on whether the second change still carries every scenario of the main specification. The scratch project was run both ways.

The second change What the tool did in the runs What the main specification held afterwards
Carried every scenario the main specification had validate passed. Archive reported "Specs updated successfully." and nothing else. The second change's wording only. The first change's wording was gone.
Omitted a scenario the first change had added validate failed. Archive stopped with "Aborted. No files were changed." The first change's requirement, unchanged, and the second change still open.

In the first run, both changes were archived. The main requirement held the second change's wording and none of the first change's wording. No output said so. A modified block gives no reason why it should: it says what the requirement is, not what changed in it.

In the second run, the first change added a scenario to the requirement. The second change was drafted before that, and it did not carry the scenario. While the first change was open, validate passed the second change. Once the first change was archived, validate failed with "MODIFIED … omits scenario(s) the current spec still has". Archive printed "Refresh the change spec before archiving to avoid dropping scenarios." and "Aborted. No files were changed.". It exited with code 1 and left the second change open. The same change passed before an archive and was refused after it.

That refusal is the only one the runs produced. Both rows agree with chapter 12's row for MODIFIED. That row says that a block must carry every scenario, and that validate and archive reject a block that drops one. The runs add one point: the check is made against the main specification as it stands on the day of the check. So the order of archiving decides whether a change is refused.

16.4 What bulk-archive adds

Section 15.5 describes bulk-archive and its rule for a conflict. Three details are relevant to the question of this chapter.

The skill defines a conflict as two or more chosen changes with delta specs for the same capability path. The unit is the path, not the requirement. So two changes that modify different requirements of one capability also count as a conflict.

For two changes that are both implemented, the skill applies them oldest first, so that the newer one overwrites the older one. For two changes that modify the same requirement, this gives the outcome of the first run in section 16.3: the main specification holds the second wording only.

The skill shows its resolution of each conflict in its table, before it asks its one confirmation question. In that table, a developer can see which change will overwrite which, before anything is written.

16.5 What verify bases its report on

Section 15.4 describes verify, its three dimensions and its severities. It leaves open what a report depends on. That is a matter of what the skill tells the agent to do.

  • For each added or modified requirement, the skill tells the agent to search the code for keywords related to it, and to "assess if implementation likely exists".
  • For each scenario, it tells the agent to check two things: whether the code handles the conditions, and whether tests exist that cover the scenario.
  • Its heuristics name the method for correctness as "keyword search, file path analysis, reasonable inference". They say not to require perfect certainty.

The skill does not tell the agent to run the code or to run a test. It asks whether a test exists. It does not ask whether the test fails when the scenario is broken.

The skill also says what a report is not. In the skill's words, a check marked "Not verified" describes a limit of the report. It is not a new condition for archive, which keeps its own checks. Two things can stop the skill. First, before the first step that writes anything, a shared project-root guard checks that the project has an OpenSpec root. When the project has none, the guard stops and asks. Second, when the change to verify is vague or ambiguous, the skill asks the user to choose one.

Verify is outside this repository's profile, which lists seven workflows. This chapter depends on the skill text of 2.1.1. It says nothing about how well an agent carries out that text.

16.6 The scenario as the unit of a check

A scenario is the unit that can be carried from the specification into a check. Chapter 6 writes it with a WHEN and a THEN that can be observed. An observable THEN is something that a test, a command or a procedure can confirm or refute. Section 8.5 asks the same of a task's evidence: that it could have come out the other way.

The tool holds no link between a scenario and a check. A specification has requirements and scenarios. It has no field for the check that covers a scenario, and a change's metadata has none either. Where the link exists, it is in the project's tests and in the tasks that name them.

16.7 Making the two comparisons

Before an archive, the developer makes the two comparisons that the tool does not make. Each comparison has a routine, like the routines of chapters 11 and 12.

Before a second archive

  1. Before archiving any change, list the active changes. Find those whose deltas name the same capability. openspec show <change> --json --deltas-only prints each delta's spec, operation, requirement name, text and scenarios.
  2. Decide which change archives first. Write the reason down in the second change's design. The order decides whose wording the main specification holds.
  3. Archive the first change, or sync it as chapter 12 describes, so that the main specification is current.
  4. For each change still open that modifies the same requirement, copy the requirement from the main specification as it now stands. The copy includes its scenarios and the first change's wording. Then apply that change's edit to the copy.
  5. Run validate on the second change.
  6. After the second archive, read the whole requirement in the main specification, not only the diff.

Step 4 does more than the refusal asks for. In a third run of the scratch project, the second change from section 16.3 was given only the scenario it had omitted. It then validated and archived. The main requirement held its wording: the first change's words "from its stock" were gone, although the first change's scenario was kept. The refusal protects a scenario, not a wording. So the wording is kept only when the first change's text is carried over as well.

Before archiving a change with code

  1. Take the delta's scenarios one at a time.
  2. For each scenario, name the check that would fail if the scenario were broken: a test, a command or a procedure.
  3. If there is no such check, write a note that says so.
  4. Run the checks.
  5. Record each result in the task that names the check, as chapter 8 describes.

16.8 Correcting the result

When a comparison finds that something is wrong, the correction depends on two things: where the error is, and how far the change has gone.

After a wrong second archive, the main specification holds a requirement that has lost the first change's wording. The archive is not edited. A new change restores the lost wording. It modifies the requirement, by the path that chapter 12 describes.

After a mismatch between the code and the specification, the skill's recommendations name the possible corrections, in these words:

  • for a requirement with no implementation: "Implement requirement X: <description>";
  • for a scenario that is not covered: "Add test or implementation for scenario: <description>";
  • for a design decision the code does not follow: "Update implementation or revise design.md to match reality".

The recommendations name the code first. Only the recommendation for a design decision offers a change to the artifact as a correction. The developer decides which side was wrong. A requirement that the code does not meet may be a missing implementation. It may also be a requirement that was not right. When the artifact is at fault and the change is open, the artifact is revised in the change, as section 11.5 says. When the requirement is archived, a new change corrects it, as chapter 12 says, and the archive is not edited.

16.9 What the example shows

The example shows a correction, and it shows neither of the two cases. The vending machine has two archived changes, give-exact-change and refuse-without-exact-change. They were never open at the same time. The second modified a requirement of the first after the first had been archived. So no order decided anything, and nothing was refused. The example holds no code. So it shows no mismatch between code and specification, and no verify report.

The tool checks the text of one change against the main specification as it stands on the day of the check. It refuses a modified requirement that has lost a scenario. It passes one that has lost another change's wording. It reads no code. Two changes can each pass and still leave a main specification that says what only one of them meant. A change can also pass with code that does something else. So whether two changes agree, and whether the code does what a scenario says, is the developer's reading. The developer reads the requirement in the main specification after the second archive. The developer also reads each scenario against the check that would fail if it were broken.

17. The Commands No Workflow Calls

Chapters 9 to 16 examined the workflows in detail. They also examined the commands that the workflows' skills tell the agent to run. The program has more commands than that. A developer runs some of them by hand, a script runs some, and some nobody needs until something goes wrong. This chapter discusses the commands that no skill runs and no earlier chapter explains. It asks each group the questions that chapter 9 asks of a workflow. Who acts? What is read and written? What can stop it? How does a reviewer judge what it did? What happens when its result is wrong? A command has no stages. So each group gets a table that fits it, in the form chapter 15 used for the workflows outside the profile. The chapter describes OpenSpec 2.1.1.

17.1 The commands that no skill runs

openspec --help lists 24 commands. The twelve skills of 2.1.1 tell the agent to run twelve of them: init, update, context, schemas, new change, status, instructions, list, show, validate, archive, and store list as the one form of store. The workflow chapters described those. No skill runs two more, and chapter 13 explains them: config, which holds the profile, and schema, which chapter 14 used to fork a schema. The others have no chapter yet. The table sorts them into four groups.

Command What it does Group
view Prints one dashboard of the specifications and the active changes. Reading the record
show --diff Shows a change with a diff of each modified requirement. Reading the record
spec, change Older forms of show, list and validate, by noun. Reading the record
templates Says where each artifact's template comes from. Checking the harness
doctor Reports the health of the root, its store and its references. Checking the harness
store Creates, registers and removes stores. Working across repositories
workset Saves named sets of folders on the machine. Working across repositories
version, install Report the program's release, and install the standalone program. The program itself
completion, feedback Add shell completion, and send feedback to the OpenSpec project. The program itself

Chapters 10 and 16 name show for other forms. --diff is the one form that no chapter has used. It belongs with the commands that read.

17.2 Reading the record

The first group reads. The developer runs each command, and the program prints. No file changes.

Command Reads Writes Can stop it
view The main specifications and the active changes. Nothing. No root.
show <change> --diff The change's proposal and deltas, and the main specification each delta names. Nothing. A name that is no change.
spec show, spec list, spec validate The main specifications. Nothing. Nothing for list: with no root it prints "No items found" and succeeds.
change show, change list, change validate The active changes. Nothing. The same as spec.

view prints a dashboard. At the top is a summary: the specifications and their requirements, the active and completed changes, and the task progress. Below it is each change, with a progress bar and the state of its artifacts. Then comes each specification, with its count of requirements. Without a terminal, view prints once and ends. It is the shortest way to see the state of a project. It says nothing that list and status do not.

show <change> --diff prints the proposal first. Then, under "Specifications Changed (diffs)", it prints a unified diff of each modified requirement against the main specification. Chapter 6 said that a reader of a modified block has to compare it with the main specification to see what changed. This form makes that comparison, for the text as it is when the command runs. It does not say that the change is right.

spec and change are the older form of the same reading, with the noun first. Each of them prints a warning that the commands are deprecated. The warning names the verb-first command to use instead: openspec show, openspec list or openspec validate. The verdicts of spec validate and change validate are those of validate. A script that still calls them works and warns. A new script has no reason to use them.

For the developer, these commands are a way to read without opening files. The review is the reading itself. Nothing in the output is a check that the earlier chapters did not describe. A dashboard full of ticks says that files exist, as status does in chapter 10.

17.3 Checking the harness

The second group checks where things come from. It reads the harness and writes nothing.

Command Reads Reports What fails it
templates The schema in use and its template files. Each artifact's template path and its source: the package, the project or the user's directory. A schema that cannot be resolved.
doctor The root, a declared store, and each entry of references in openspec/config.yaml. Whether each is found and healthy, with a fix for each problem. Not a missing reference: that is a warning.
store doctor <id> One registered store. Its location, its OpenSpec root, its metadata and its Git state. A store that is not registered.

Chapter 13 asked of a schema where it comes from, with openspec schema which. templates answers the same question for the files below the schema. In a project that has not forked its schema, every template comes from the package. In a project with a fork, the same command names the project as the source.

doctor looks at relations, not at content. With nothing declared, it reports the root and says that no references are declared. A reference may have a store that is not registered on the machine. doctor reports it as unregistered, with the command that would register it, and still exits with status 0. A warning is printed and not counted. A script may run doctor and check only its exit status; it learns only that the command ran. To learn what the command found, it has to read the --json output.

For the developer, the two commands are the answer when an agent was told something other than expected. A rule may not appear, a template may not match, or a reference may add nothing to the instructions. The cause is in one of the places these commands name.

17.4 Working across repositories

The third group writes, and it writes on the machine. Chapter 3 said that the program keeps stores and the user's own state outside the repository. These are the commands that create that state. OpenSpec's guide calls stores and worksets a beta. It says that their commands, flags and file formats may change between releases.

A store is a standalone OpenSpec repository, registered on the machine under an id. It moves the openspec/ folder out of a code repository into a repository of its own. Several code repositories can then share one set of specifications. Any command that reads or writes specifications and changes takes --store <id>. With it, the command works on the store instead of the nearest openspec/ folder. Its output then begins with "Using OpenSpec root:" and the store's id.

Command Writes Can stop it
store setup <id> --path <folder> The folder, with openspec/, an .openspec-store/store.yaml file, a Git repository and a first commit; and the store's entry in the machine's registry. No Git identity, unless told to skip Git.
store register <path> The entry in the registry, for a store that already exists. A folder without an openspec/ root.
store unregister <id> Removes the entry. The files stay. An id that is not registered.
store remove <id> --yes Removes the entry and deletes the folder. No --yes with no one to ask.
workset create <name> --member <folder> A named list of folders, in the user's data directory. No member.
workset remove <name> --yes Removes the list. The member folders are not touched. No --yes with no one to ask.

store setup writes in two places. The first is the store's folder. The second is its entry in the machine's registry, which is in the user's data directory, next to the list of projects the program knows. store unregister removes only the entry and leaves the files where they are. store remove deletes the folder as well. With no one to ask, it does so only when --yes is given.

A project points at a store in two ways. The first is a store key in its configuration. It makes the store the root when the project's own openspec/ holds no specifications or changes. When openspec/ holds them, the program ignores the key with a warning. The second is a references list. It does not change the root. It adds an index of each store's specifications to every instruction, in a block marked "Read-only upstream context". The index gives each specification's Purpose and the command to fetch it in full. The agent is told that the store exists. It is not told to obey it, and nothing checks whether it read it.

The program decides where a command works in a fixed order, and the first rule that applies wins. First is --store on the command. Second is the project's own openspec/, when it holds specifications or changes. Third is the store key. Fourth is a defaultStore in the global configuration, which config sets. When none applies, the command fails and lists the registered stores. It does not choose a store by its name, even one that matches the repository's name.

In a store, the workflows run as they always do; only the place changes. A developer may start a change from a code repository that uses a store. The change is then written into the store's folder, with all its artifacts and, at the end, its archive. The code it describes stays in the code repository. The two are committed and pushed separately, and no check compares them.

The skills follow the same rule. Each skill that the book's profile installs has a paragraph on store selection. The developer may name a store, or the work may be in one. Then the agent runs store list --json for the registered ids. It adds --store <id> to every command that reads or writes specifications and changes, for the rest of the workflow. The project may declare a store that this machine cannot resolve. Then the agent stops before writing and shows the error and its fix. It does not treat the project as one without OpenSpec. That is why store list is the one form of store that a skill runs.

A workset is a name for several folders, kept on the machine. workset open writes a workspace file and opens the folders in one editor window. The guide says that the openers for two editors are built in. It says that the openers for terminal agents are disabled for now. workset remove removes the list and does not touch the member folders. A workset does not change which openspec/ folder a command uses.

For the developer, the review of this group is a review of the machine. The registry and the worksets are files outside every repository. OpenSpec never clones, pulls or pushes a store. A teammate clones it with Git and registers it on each machine. A checkout that was not pulled shows old specifications until it is pulled. A teammate who clones only the project does not have the store. That is why doctor reports a reference as unregistered on a new machine. Only two commands touch a folder: store setup creates one, and store remove --yes deletes one.

17.5 The program itself

The fourth group is about the program, and its effects go furthest: most of its forms change the machine or send something off it.

Command Reaches
version Nothing outside the program.
version --check The package registry, for a newer release.
install [version] The project's GitHub releases, for the standalone program.
completion generate <shell> Nothing; it prints a script.
completion install <shell> The shell's own setup files.
feedback <message> GitHub, as a public issue on the OpenSpec project.

version prints the release, the package manager and the scope of the install. Its --json form adds the folder of the install. Chapter 3 says that the README names the release, and this is the line it points at. version --check asks the registry whether a newer release exists. update does the same when it offers an upgrade.

install fetches the standalone program from the project's GitHub release, together with its checksums. The standalone program runs without Node.js. install puts it in ~/.local/bin unless told otherwise. It then says which copy comes first on the path. It also prints the command that removes the package-manager copy. Until one of the two is removed, the machine has two programs, and version says which one ran.

completion generate <shell> prints a completion script for the shell. completion install writes such a script into the shell's setup, and completion uninstall removes it.

feedback sends a message to the OpenSpec project. When the gh program is installed and signed in, feedback uses it to file an issue on the project's GitHub repository. It adds the release, the platform and the time below the message. Without gh, it prints a prefilled address for the issue form instead. An issue on a public repository is public.

For the developer, this group is the one whose effect is outside the project. Before a run, the question is where the command reaches: the shell, the install, or a public tracker.

17.6 Judging the result, and correcting it

The program checks none of the effects of these commands. It reads, it reports, and it writes what it is told. The checks of form in the earlier chapters are the only checks there are. What a wrong run costs depends on what it wrote:

  • A reading or checking command changes no file, so a wrong run costs a second run with the right name or form.
  • A warning from doctor is read and not counted, so a gate that depends on its exit status passes a missing reference.
  • store unregister and workset remove are undone by registering the store or creating the workset again, because their files were left in place.
  • store remove --yes deletes the folder. Only a copy elsewhere, such as a pushed remote, brings it back.
  • A store checkout that was not pulled shows old specifications, and the agent works against them. OpenSpec never pulls a store, so only pulling it with Git brings it up to date.
  • install leaves two copies of the program until one is removed, and the path decides which runs.
  • A feedback issue is public once it is filed. Correcting it is a matter for the tracker, not for the program.

Before a command of the third or fourth group, the developer can say in one sentence what it will write and where. Afterwards, the developer can run git status and the matching list: store list, workset list or version.

The commands that no workflow calls read the record, check the harness, connect repositories and maintain the program. None of them judges a change. Reading and checking leave the project as it was, and say nothing that validate, list and status do not. Connecting writes the machine's state, which no clone carries and which doctor can find missing. Maintaining reaches the shell, the install and a public tracker. So the developer's review of these commands is not a review of a change. It is a review of the machine they wrote to, and of what left it.

18. What the Book Describes, and What It Leaves Open

The book has followed one tool from its conventions to the commands that no workflow calls. This last chapter says what kind of book that makes it and what it found. It also names the questions it leaves for the reader to continue. It adds nothing about the tool that an earlier chapter did not establish. It answers none of the questions it names.

18.1 What kind of book this is

The first two chapters are about the method, not the tool. Chapter 1 argued that work done with a model needs a record that outlives the conversation. It also argued that the record has a cost, and that the record must be worth that cost. Chapter 2 named the cornerstones that such a record must satisfy. OpenSpec appeared there as one implementation, and section 1.6 said that it is replaceable in the argument.

From chapter 3 on, the book is a technical description of one tool in one release, OpenSpec 2.1.1. It describes what the tool writes, what it reads, what it checks and what it leaves to the developer. It describes these in the order in which a change meets them.

Chapters What they describe
3 How OpenSpec's conventions carry the cornerstones, and where they stop.
4 to 8 One change from request to archive, and each of its four artifacts: the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks.
9 to 12 The workflows of the book's profile, and the validate command, ordered by who does the work in each.
13 and 14 Customizing the harness, and one customized change from fork to archive.
15 to 17 The five workflows outside the profile, the two comparisons that no check makes, and the commands that no workflow calls.

It is not a manual of every option the tool has. It is not a guide to practice either. It says how the tool behaves when a developer uses it. It does not say how a team should organise its work around the tool.

18.2 The one finding

Chapter after chapter reached the same result. validate checks the form of a delta and of the main specifications. It does not check whether the behaviour is the right one. The program counts the tasks and does not read them, so a ticked box is a claim. No check opens the proposal or the design. The program sees the planning workflows only as files that exist. The program confirms that a customization is well formed, but it does not confirm its effect. No check compares two changes with each other, or a scenario with the code. The commands that no workflow calls read, check, connect and maintain. None of them judges a change.

That is one finding, seen from every side: the program checks form and counts, and the developer judges content. Chapter 9 described it as a division of work. In that division, the agent writes, the program reports and checks, and the developer decides and reviews. Chapter 3 gave the reason for it. Human control is the one cornerstone that the conventions cannot carry, because a tool can hold a decision but cannot make one. Everything the book said about reviewing an artifact, a workflow or a command applies that division to one part of the tool.

18.3 What the book leaves open

The questions below follow from what the book showed. Each names the chapter whose finding it extends. None is answered here, because the book has no evidence to answer it with.

Large projects

  • Where does a capability end? The example has one capability, and section 5.5 showed how a proposal names the capability it changes. A system with dozens of capabilities needs a rule for dividing behaviour into capabilities. The book has no such rule to offer.
  • Who reads two changes against each other? Chapter 16 showed that no check compares two changes that are open at the same time. It also showed that the comparison is a reading of the main specification after the second archive. With one writer, that reading is a habit. With many active changes, it is a duty that someone has to own, at a time that the process has to fix. The book does not say who, or when.
  • How is a specification shared? Section 17.4 described stores. A store is a repository of specifications that several code repositories can use. It is registered on each machine, OpenSpec never synchronises it, and it is marked as beta. The section described the commands, not a practice. The book does not show how a store is kept current or who may change it. It also does not show how a change to a store is coordinated with the code that the store describes.
  • Who owns the record? Chapter 5 said that an agent drafts a proposal and a person owns it. Sections 1.7 and 2.7 said that a team must decide what is worth a record. The book has one owner throughout. It does not show how a team settles either question.
  • How does a change meet a branch and a review? The book never relates a change folder to a branch, a pull request or a code review. The only exception is the remark in section 3.4 that an abandoned change leaves no half-finished branch behind. The book does not describe whether a change is in one branch. It also does not describe who approves its artifacts, or in which order they are reviewed against the code.
  • What does automation check? Chapter 11 showed what validate checks. Section 17.3 showed that doctor exits with status 0 on a warning. The book does not describe whether either should stop a merge. It also does not describe what a pipeline would need to read to stop it.

Introducing and keeping it

  • How does a system without specifications get them? Section 15.6 showed onboard doing one change on a real task in an existing project. The book does not show how to write the main specifications of a system that has none, from code that already runs.
  • How does a project move between releases? The book moved from 2.0.0 to 2.1.1. It noted the differences where they mattered, in sections 3.1 and 9.2. It does not show how a project with many changes moves its artifacts and its skills through a release.
  • How fast does a specification drift? Section 2.6 said that a specification must be maintained. Section 3.7 said that nothing checks afterwards whether the specification and the code still agree. The book observed no project for long enough to see drift happen.
  • What does it cost, and what does it return? Sections 1.7 and 1.8 described the shape of the cost. They said that the size of the return is not established. The book measured neither.

Comparisons

  • Would another spec-driven tool behave differently? Section 1.6 said that another tool may use different names, different artifacts and a different way of working. Chapter 3 said that a different tool could arrange the same material and still serve the same principles. The book describes how OpenSpec divides the work between the agent, the program and the developer. It does not show how another tool divides it.
  • Would another spec-driven tool check more? Section 1.6 said that OpenSpec is replaceable in the argument, and the book compares it with nothing. The finding of section 18.2 is a finding about OpenSpec 2.1.1. Whether another tool closes any part of that gap is open.

None of these questions is a defect found in the tool. Where OpenSpec has a mechanism for one of them, the book has described the mechanism. An example is stores for shared specifications. What the book has not done is use the mechanism where many people, many changes and many months meet. That is where these questions are decided.

The book has shown what OpenSpec writes, what it checks and what it leaves to the developer, for one release. The answer was the same in every chapter: the program checks form and counts, and the developer judges the content. The book does not say what happens where many people, many changes and many months meet. Instead, it passes to the reader the questions that follow from its finding: who reads, who owns, what is shared, and what is checked. The tool will not answer them, because each depends on a reading of content. That reading is the part of the work that stays with the developer.
